speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the emergency amendments to the Energy Administration Act regarding natural gas pricing.
On October 31, 1985, the federal Government and the oil and gas producing provinces of Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan signed the agreement on natural gas markets and prices. The objective is to make an orderly transition to a competitive market for natural gas by November 1, 1986.
Since 1975, the wholesale price for natural gas sold in interprovincial trade has been set by Governments under federal-provincial energy agreements. The federal and provincial Governments are now working hard to amend legislation required to meet the objectives of market sensitive pricing by November 1. Alberta, for example, has prepared extensive amendments to its legislation to ensure that the objective of the agreement is met in the province.
Provincial Governments have also taken steps necessary to facilitate direct sales between producers and consumers, and have undertaken competitive marketing programs during the transition year. In both Ontario and Quebec the provincial regulatory boards have taken major steps to ensure that large consumers can have open access to distribution systems.
The emergency Bill to amend the Energy Administration Act is needed to fulfil the Government of Canada's commitments under the national gas agreement. The Bill will permit the Governor in Council to continue to approve negotiated domestic natural gas prices during this transition period. It will also remove any ambiguity surrounding natural gas pricing arrangements that have already been negotiated. Without these amendments the agreement on natural gas markets and prices, signed on October 31, 1985, could be in jeopardy. With these amendments the policy of negotiated prices for domestic gas prices could be halted. Without negotiated prices western natural gas producers could not effectively compete in the market-place and could lose sales to competing fuels, including imported oil. Loss of sales, particularly in the key industrial market segment, would create economic hardships for the west. Large eastern Canadian gas consumers would be denied access to attractively priced domestic natural gas supplies. To date large petrochemical, manufacturing, mining and forest product companies have negotiated natural gas cost savings in excess of $100 million.
My Minister's Department has received full support for these amendments from other Government Departments and agencies, including the National Energy Board. The industry, along with the producing and consuming provinces, want the ambiguities removed and the regulated process streamlined. These amendments will meet their concerns. This Bill does not introduce any new policy initiatives, but its passage is important to all Canadians.
Since last October Canada's natural gas marketers have been busy negotiating contracts that benefit both the producers and the consumers. When you stop to think of it, who ever heard of a natural gas marketer in Canada before last year. There may have been a few, but there are certainly more people working in the natural gas business today than ever before. You ask why? Governments are getting out of the gas pricing business during the transition year. Producers can now go out and sell their product. The prices for natural gas in Canada are now established in the market-place where they should be. Natural gas is now able to compete with other fuels for market share. By November 1 of this year all natural gas services will be negotiated in the market.
These changes could not have been introduced at a better time. Imagine the position our natural gas industry would be in if it continued to be tied to Government regulated prices at a time when oil prices have fallen. How could natural gas compete in a market where the dual fuel capacity of industrial consumers provides the flexibility to switch to a competing fuel source including imported oil. How could gas consumers benefit from a lower energy cost? Natural gas must be competitive and the federal-provincial agreement signed last year allows this to happen.
This agreement received my full support when it was signed last October. The changes to the Energy Administration Act before the House today, which allows a wide variety of negotiated arrangements, streamlining the regulatory process
June 26, 1986

during this transition year, also have my complete support. I respectfully request the approval of the House for this emergency Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I want to support the Parliamentary Secretary in his request for approval on all sides of the House for this emergency Bill. While I certainly agree with that request, I want to say a few words in order to underline the importance of deleting the ambiguities that presently exist in the natural gas marketing network.
Natural gas marketing and distribution is not an easy subject to understand at the best of times. However, in this transition year from October 31, 1985 to November 1, 1986 there are many ambiguities and many questions, not only in the minds of industry but consumers as well. Hopefully, these mysteries will be eased by this legislation, Bill C-112.
On October 31 the Minister promised a new era for consumers and producers which would be brought about by market sensitive pricing. She said that the pricing would, in effect, provide gradual deregulation during the transition period when the Alberta border and Toronto wholesale prices would be frozen at existing levels. Although this is happening, the problem is that it is not working out the way we had hoped.
I believe the National Energy Board has acted very responsibly and made some very good decisions in the best interests of the country. They have unravelled a good deal of the mystery in this transition period and in the natural gas deregulation and marketing problems. The National Energy Board has stated that with respect to TransCanada PipeLines, private contracts between buyers and sellers will have priority. That is important because there are many bulk purchasers of natural gas in central Canada who will benefit from these private contracts and individual contracts between the buyer and seller. TransCanada PipeLines is no longer in the position of having to be the seller, but in this case can be simply the carrier. That is a step in the right direction.
However, the problem still exists for the small consumer such as the homeowner and the small businessman. They cannot get this preferential treatment through the TransCanada PipeLines. They are unable to organize a special agreement between buyer and seller and receive this preferential status with TransCanada PipeLines. While there will be large reductions in the price of natural gas for the large consumer, I am very much concerned that there will not be much in the way of price decreases for the small consumer, if there are any at all. I hope the Government will take this into consideration because it is not long until November 1.
The other feature deals with what I would call the adjacent border price, whereby natural gas can be sold into the United States, but not at a price lower than that available to Canadians in the area where the natural gas crosses the Canada-U.S. border.
Energy Administration Act
Currently, through the regulated system, the National Energy Board can tell us the exact prices in particular areas because it is documented, largely through the TransCanada PipeLines system. However, what will happen when there are private contracts between sellers and purchasers, particularly large purchasers? This information will not be available to the National Energy Board and I am afraid that the NEB will not have the information upon which to base this adjacent border price. There will be some slippage and consumers in Canada will not be assured that they are getting the benefit of the low prices that Americans will receive. This may not be intentional on the part of the Government, but it can happen and we should correct that situation.
In committee, the National Energy Board and the Chairman in particular said that the Board will need new terms of reference prior to November 1, 1986 in order to be able to deal with this new method of selling and marketing natural gas in this country, and in order to ensure that Canadian consumers in central Canada will receive as low a price as American buyers. I hope that the Government will address this question.
Now that Bill C-112 will eliminate these ambiguities, further policies can be brought into effect so that people in this country, particularly consumers in central Canada, will know where they stand and will have the benefit of the lower prices they should be receiving.

Mr. Speaker, as my Party's energy critic, I want to make a few remarks on this Bill. I support its speedy passage. I accept the Parliamentary Secretary's assertion that this Bill would help an orderly transition toward deregulation of the natural gas market by November 1.
This is a very complicated area. One wonders whether one is reading English when trying to understand this material. However, when one recalls that certain principles are involved, the complications of the natural gas market disappear and what is involved becomes rather clear.
When the Government decided to deregulate the price and marketing of natural gas, it had to deal with many contacts already in existence, including some famous take or pay contracts held by TransCanada PipeLines. The Government had to deal with distribution and the interests of producers, consumers and transporters. It seemed that the Government handed this question to the National Energy Board, for it to attempt to unravel the Gordian knot. As my friend, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) said, the Board did a good job in trying to deal with that issue. I agree with that statement because it is a difficult issue. While I do not believe anyone is completely happy with the decision, that would have been impossible to achieve.
This is a difficult issue because the interests of producers, shippers and distributors are involved. It is worth a lot of money because Canada exports some $4 billion a year in natural gas to the United States. That is about 5 per cent of

June 26, 1986
Energy Administration Act
the American market, which means a lot of money for western Canadian producers.
In my remarks I want to outline some of the issues and principles that should be recognized. The first issue is U.S. exports. Natural gas is a non-renewable resource that is clean burning and can be used in many different ways. The problem is that we will deplete our natural gas resource in Alberta, British Columbia and parts of Saskatchewan and will have to go to the frontiers to look for gas there. Your Honour knows what will happen. The cost will dramatically increase for the consumer. Here in Ontario, where we are right now, where many people heat their homes and cook by natural gas, in an expanding market, we must ensure that we do not export all our cheap, non-renewable natural gas at fire-sale prices because there is an opportunity in the American market and we want to grab that. Producers will always say to regulatory boards like the National Energy Board and the Government,"We want to export more if we can because we need the cash flow and then we will reinvest and we will find more gas", and so on. That is true in some ways, but in other ways, when it is a depleting resource, gas will be found in more and more difficult places. It will cost more to transport and will mean higher prices for consumers.
I am proud that the NDP has taken the same position federally, here in Ontario, in the House of Commons, as it took in Alberta. I will refer to a policy statement by the Leader of the Official Opposition in Your Honour's province of Alberta, by the Hon. Ray Martin, who is a New Democrat. He said:
It should first of all be stressed that New Democrats have never seen the"Brick Warehouse firesale" approach of wholesale exports at the cheapest price possible as any sort of sensible solution to the problems of our natural gas industry. Far better, we have argued, to look at the big picture through a greater emphasis on use of this non-renewable resource here in western Canada, as well as through changes in our pricing and distribution systems which benefit the many small Canadian producers operating here. In this regard, we have advocated gas prorationing, gas banking, encouragement of M-Gas and other plants for production of gasoline from natural gas, natural gas substitution for provincial government vehicle fuel and other measures to enhance markets locally.
I have often thought over the years, if I can digress for a minute, that perhaps the little green buses on which we come to the House that burn the oil, should perhaps have been converted to natural gas, as has been done in many companies in Vancouver and with municipal vehicles. In other words, here is the Leader of the New Democratic Party in Alberta saying in Alberta, "Let us not sell out all our gas right now at fire-sale prices". That is not to say we should not export gas. We must export some gas because we must keep the small producers going and we do have a surplus, but we must be very careful that we do not sell it at fire-sale prices. That is not the situation right at the moment, because there is a gas bubble in the United States. Spot prices in the United States have gone down as low as about $2 a thousand cubic feet, recently. However, we must be careful not to export for a quick buck.
The second principle to be kept in mind is that we must try to receive the best possible prices for the consumers. Access must be given to small producers. Let me explain the consumers' part, first. The Government must continue to follow the principle that we should not be selling Canadian gas to American consumers at prices lower than we sell to Canadians. I know there are problems involving transportation charges, distances, that can be adjusted at the borders and areas adjacent to the United States. Basically, we should keep to that principle and I hope the Government will not abandon it. If it does, it can look to us over here to raise it as a political issue. We must give the small producers access to the pipelines and to the markets. That is what members of the NDP in Alberta were saying when they spoke of pro-rationing and so on. The TransCanada PipeLines had a monopoly, one pipeline going from the West to the East, carrying the gas. Contracts were being made for buying gas, and it was being transported and sold. Gas could be purchased quite cheaply from small producers who were desperate for the money, because Trans-Canada PipeLines had the only access to the pipeline.
As I have advocated in the House over the last few years, we in the NDP feel that the monopoly of TransCanada PipeLines should be broken up or, alternatively, be taken over as a public enterprise. I notice that the National Energy Board did this to some extent in its decision giving producers access to the pipeline. That was a really important step because there cannot be a deregulated, competitive market without there being a deregulated, competitive system.
That is the mistake the Government made in deregulating crude oil. The Government said it would deregulate crude oil under the Western Accord and that it would help consumers and producers. Because there are four or five companies that control most of the transporting, refining and marketing, we ended up having the worst of all possible worlds; that is, consumers paying more than world price. Just look at what Americans pay for gasoline compared to Canadians. Small producers in Alberta are going under because they are selling their oil at the lowest possible price, lower than world price. We do not want to see that with natural gas. We want to see a system where there will be some control over exports and there will be fair prices to consumers. We are worried, with the new deal to which the National Energy Board agreed, that the residential consumer will still not benefit as much as we think possible. Prices should be lower for consumers because the price of oil has come down and the price of natural gas should follow.
I want to say one word about Quebec. Concerning deregulation, we think there would have been a much more positive impact upon Quebec industry and residential consumers had it not been for the Conservative decision last November to cut back funding for new laterals, gas laterals, so that natural gas could be brought into all these Quebec communities. We will be pushing for the federal Government to take further action to develop Quebec and Atlantic markets for gas, both for
June 26, 1986

national energy security reasons and also to provide a market for domestic producers.
[ Translation]
I would much rather have a deal between Alberta producers and Quebec consumers, which is better than a sale or contract between Alberta producers and the Americans. This would also be in the interest of Canadian energy security. We in the New Democratic Party of Canada are in favour of expanded market in the Province of Quebec, and we deplore the fact that the Conservative Government did not promote the extension of the gas pipeline further than Quebec.

Perhaps I can end by telling the Government that we will watch this deregulation in November and we hope it will be much better than what the Government has done in trying to deregulate the price of crude oil under the Western Accord, which we consider right now not to be a success, because we think that the ordinary Canadian consumer has not benefited as much as he or she should, nor has the ordinary small producer in Canada. We hope that a different result can be achieved for natural gas. That is why we are pleased to help this Government today by passing this Bill as an interim measure.

What I have to say is that the commission was looking into the advisability of building a large-diameter pipeline to carry natural gas from the Mackenzie Delta, from Prudhoe Bay in Alaska, down through Canada to the lower 48 states. The commission received a great deal of criticism from the industry and people around at the time for recommending a 10-year delay, for various reasons, in building the pipeline.
I wish to say for the record that I have now found what the spot price of natural gas is, something to which I referred in my speech on second reading. It is now something in the order of $2.30 per 1,000 cubic feet in the United States. The pipeline would have carried gas at about $8 to $10 per 1,000 cubic feet. One can imagine how many broke companies we would have had in Canada had the pipeline gone ahead.
Not only did the report of the Berger Commission enhance and stimulate the environmental movement in Canada, and not only was it receptive to the growing native movement and the assertion of small business people to get a piece of the action in industrial developments and megaprojects, but it also helped the big oil and gas companies which would have gone broke had they built the pipeline. It will be built some day because we will run out of natural gas eventually in southern Canada. Let us hope that by the time it is built it will be built by consensus and to the benefit of the people who live in the North, as well as to the consumers who live in southern Canada and the businesses who will build it.

The House resumed from Friday, June 20, 1986, consideration in Committee of Bill C-l 17, an Act to facilitate financial arrangements between farmers and their creditors-Mr. Wise-Mr. Paproski in the Chair; and on the amendment (Mr. Foster) (p. 14801).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. May I ask Members to please take their seats. The House is again in Committee of the Whole on Bill C-l 17, an Act to facilitate financial arrangements betwen farmers and their creditors. When the Committee rose on Friday last Clause 33 of the Bill with an amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) was under consideration. The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) had the floor. I will recognize the Hon. Member for Algoma.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment which I proposed was to Clause 33. It reads as follows:
Where in the opinion of a review panel, a satisfactory arrangement cannot be reached without injustice or undue delay, it shall report its finding to the Board and the Board may refer the matter to a court of competent jurisdiction to formulate the arrangement that it deems equitable under the circumstances.
I proposed that amendment because under this Bill is that the review board really has no effective means of effecting a negotiated arrangement between farmer and creditor. Even where a bank or other lending institution has changed the
arrangement or done something markedly unjust to the producer, the review panel has no power to take action. The amendment is not proposed to provide an automatic court review. It simply provides that where there is an injustice or undue delay, the panel can recommend that to the board and the board may refer it to a court of competent jurisdiction.
The concern expressed by agricultural producers across this country is that under the Bill the way it is now drafted a creditor can petition the farmer into a review. Mind you, he has to have the permission of the farmer. However, can you imagine the situation where a chartered bank has called on the review board to undertake a review of the farmer's debts and the farmer refused? He really cannot refuse. In the review itself he is sworn to secrecy, as are the panelists and the creditors. Pressure is brought to bear. The banks or other creditors can sit on their hands for up to 120 days if they can persuade the board to extend the time. Then the whole exercise is over. There is no review by Parliament or anyone else of how the system is working.
If we do not take this action we are saying to the farmers concerned, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has estimated there are 8,000 of them and there may be more, that even where the bank is doing something improper or unjust, the panel will have no power to recommend court or other action. In fact, it is worse than that. They cannot even talk about it outside of the hearing.
This procedure is essential to the proper functioning of the review panel. I have talked with the chairman of the Grey-Bruce pilot project. He spent about five or six months on this, along with a half a dozen farmers and other people knowledgeable and concerned about the crisis. In his opinion there was no way this process would work unless there was a means by which a matter could be referred to a court of competent jurisdiction. In fact, if this amendment is not adopted by the Minister I believe the whole system will stall. We will have thousands of applications to review boards, the farmer will make representations to the creditor in order to reach an arrangement, and it will simply be a case of the review board jaw-boning or arm-twisting. I do not know about you, Mr. Chairman, but I have not had much luck jaw-boning or armtwisting any bankers I know. I do not think farmers facing this situation will have much more luck either.
The other thing that is developing is that other provinces have enacted legislation. For example, in Saskatchewan a farmer goes before a debt review board and the option is there to refer the matter to a court if no agreement can be reached. Clearly the Premier of that province, who views the situation so seriously that he took on the responsibility of being Minister of Agriculture, made it clear in a press statement a week or so ago that if this legislation is not made stronger he will not use it. He will maintain the existing legislation. The same thing is happening in Manitoba. They have introduced legislation which will give them the option of a court review.
It is for those reasons I think this amendment is absolutely essential, not only to make these boards effective but also to

June 26, 1986

have a uniform policy under the constitutional authority of the federal Government in regard to bankruptcy. If you look at this legislation in the first paragraph, it deals with the interpretation of an insolvent farmer. The three items referred to are taken directly from the bankruptcy laws of this country. It is under those provisions that this legislation is brought in, although the word "bankruptcy" is not used in the Bill itself.
It is also important that we do not build up a patchwork of legislation. Provincial Governments other than Manitoba and Saskatchewan are going to be under great pressure to do the same thing as those two provinces if we do not make this provision available.
Over the weekend and during the days since this Bill was last before the House I received encouragement and support from the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture, the president of the National Farmers' Union, the Women's Group for Farm Survival in eastern Ontario, individual farmers, and people who served on the Grey-Bruce pilot project. There has been a great deal of support. I have a letter from Reverend Howard Brox, the General Secretary of the United Church of Canada, dated June 24, 1986 in which says with regard to Farm Debt Review Boards:
The Division of Mission in Canada requests the legislation either be amended to include an effective enforcing role for the review boards or be referred back to the Standing Committee on Agriculture for strengthening.
The concern of the church is for farm families caught in the midst of this farm crisis and we do not believe that the legislation, as it presently stands, will aid them. In fact, those same farm families may be hurt even more if the legislation is not changed so as to strengthen the power of the farm review boards to enforce their recommendations.
I have stronger evidence that this provision is essential. I have in my hand an article from the London Free Press of last July 11 in which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) himself says that it is essential that this legislation be brought in, that it must be done under the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act, and he indicated his support for reference to a court.
This amendment which I am proposing is not nearly as strong as that because we are not operating under the Bankruptcy Act itself. Under this Bill this is a stand-alone board, but the amendment does propose that where there is, in the opinion of the review panel, injustice or undue delay about to occur, the matter, with the support of the review board for the province or region, can be referred to a court of competent jurisdiction to formulate the arrangement that it deems equitable under the circumstances.
I know that some groups, like the cattlemen, have argued that having this provision will be harmful to farm credit. I simply refer them and other groups like that to the fact that Saskatchewan has had in place a moratorium for almost a year and a half now. They have had the same provision, really a stronger provision than this, in their legislation where when review panels cannot reach an agreement they can refer it to a court of competent jurisdiction. The credit levels there are no
Farm Debt Review Act
tougher or easier than they are in other regions of the country. Clearly the Manitoba legislation will do the same thing.
I would certainly hope that the Minister will look at this amendment, as he promised to do last Friday, with a view to giving it his support.
There is no doubt that the Minister can, under Section 10, establish regulations or rules outlining the circumstances under which references could be made to a court, or if during the first six months or longer period he feels there should be no references to the court of the operation while the whole system shakes down, that would be the Minister's prerogative.
I think that this amendment is essential so that we have one uniform system across the country without a patchwork of provincial laws applying in various ways and giving unequal justice across the country. I think it is essential that the review panels can proceed to negotiate agreements, and when they come across injustice or improper behaviour by a lending institution and the lending institution is not willing to make it right, and are adamant in that regard, then they can recommend to the review board to refer the matter to a court for their consideration.
I would hope, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister would accept this recommendation so that the whole system will be that much more effective, and that we see justice done to the thousands of farmers who are facing serious financial difficulty, or insolvency.
We know that there is going to be perhaps the most dramatic, the most serious restructuring of farm debt in the next two years that we have seen since the 1930s. We know there are thousands of farmers who six or seven years ago had land that was worth $3,000 an acre. It is now worth a thousand dollars an acre. We know that that is common in southwestern Ontario. We know in places like the Peace River where land was worth $800 an acre five or six years ago it is worth $275. We know that certain unscrupulous individuals are waiting until it is down from $275 to $100 an acre to snap it up.
I think it is important that as this massive restructuring of the farm debt takes place we not only do justice to the banks and the lending institutions, but that we do justice to the farmers, especially the young farmers who bought farms in the late 1970s and the farm value per acre drop dramatically and have seen their equity wiped out. They should be given a fair chance to end up operating those farms, that they are not dealt off to the banks or to other lending institutions whose interests are not necessarily in the community itself, but are responding to demands from headquarters in Toronto or some other capital city in our country.
I would hope that the Minister and the members of his caucus would consider this amendment. I put it in good faith believing that there is strong support for it in the country, and believing that it will be a good safety valve for cases where injustice is being done to a farmer. The review panels really want to see action taken to redress those injustices.

Mr. Chairman, I listened very carefully to the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). He has given a very good speech. He is dealing with a very important subject. I think that those of us who have had any connection with the financial difficulties in the agricultural industry and have communicated with individuals and farm organizations across the country in the last year or year and a half will know that this particular issue has not just been debated in the House of Commons in the last 20 minutes, but rather has been first and foremost in the public forum, particularly in agricultural organizations for the last year or year and a half.
What we are considering here is whether or not to decide- and I know that the Hon. Member has some conditions attached-to extend the power and the authority in legislation to a court or to a review panel to unilaterally write down debt.
I did say and have said many times, perhaps beginning last June and July-maybe even in September-that I thought that perhaps where every effort was made on a voluntary basis by a review panel and that a decision could not be reached then those cases should indeed be referred to a court.
After making that statement I got the message loud and clear from across the country, from all sectors, all regions, indeed from within the membership of the various organizations which actually took a public position asking for such powers, that we should be aware of that. We should not ignore the fact that the provinces will not accept that at this time.
The Hon. Member talks about the need for a uniform program to apply across the country. We are required to do that in order to be consistent with the Constitution and the Charter of Rights. Therefore, if we moved in that direction we would not achieve that, because I believe, with one or two exceptions, that all of the other provinces would reject it. We would not be doing a service there at all.
I do not want to rule out that change in the future because the Hon. Member will know, as will the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, that we have had some discussion following our last exchange in Committee of the Whole. They know I have accepted some of their amendments, and I believe there are one or two others that I will accept. As well, I will be moving a Government amendment that was really put forward by the Hon. Member for Humbolt-Lake Centre. It refers to the type of review we do.
I firmly believe that there is no question that this is an important issue. However, the proper and appropriate place for careful consideration of this particular issue of extending the power of the court or review panel should be made at the time we review the progress or lack thereof of the review panel and the legislation. That will take place in the appropriate forum, either a legislative committee or standing committee of the House. Given the new powers and authority of the committees, witnesses can appear from across Canada and those committee can deal directly and specifically with that issue. There is no
question that it will be the issue. It has been debated in the past and will continue to be debated, even when the legislation is in place and the review boards are operating. We can have a track record and something to review. I am certain that this would be the more appropriate time to review this particular amendment which the Hon. Member is suggesting.
I think we have lost sight of something here. We have lost sight of the fact that we assume that the success rate flowing to farmers will be higher through a court process. I do not believe that. There is certainly more goodwill within the banking community than there was 20 months ago, but how much there is, I am not sure. I expect that it has greatly improved, but we will know that until these review panels have an opportunity to work. I firmly believe that our success rate will be higher under the voluntary process than through cases being decided by the courts.
I cannot accept this amendment and the Hon. Member knows that from the discussions we have had. However, I do not want to leave the impression that we are throwing it out forever. We do not know what we might have to do in this and other areas to continue our support for the agricultural industry in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to add a few words with respect to this amendment that was proposed by my very distinguished colleague, the Member for Algoma.
As the Minister knows, my colleague is not suggesting that the farmer would be asking the courts to take over. He is suggesting that the board be given that prerogative if and when there is an injustice being committed in the eyes of the board. This board is not appointed by opposition Members of the House, or even by the aggrieved farmer or the banker in question. The board is appointed pursuant to this Bill, which is by Order-in-Council, if I read the Bill properly. This means that the Minister will probably personally choose the people who will sit on that board. I trust that they will be people with good and appropriate judgment and will exercise that judgment in an effective manner.
Therefore, I am at a loss to understand why the Minister does not want to give this alternative, which is not necessarily an option in every case, to a board which he appoints by Order-in-Council. While there are parliamentary reviews of Order-in-Council appointments, it is the Minister who will appoint this board. This board is already given the authority to adjudicate in these matters. Yet the Minister refuses to give the board the privilege, when appropriate and necessary, not to judge it again but to ask the courts to do so, if it feels it is in the best interests of the case. I believe this is basically a friendly amendment which does not really challenge what the Minister is attempting to do. I believe we are striving for the same goals, but I am in some difficulty understanding why the Minister does not want to give this board the power, when deemed appropriate, to refer this kind of matter to a court. It is the job of the court to adjudicate in such matters.

The Minister said in his reply to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma, that perhaps there are occasions when courts will not be as effective in dealing with these kinds of matters as the board itself. Surely, when a board believes that the outcome of a case can be enhanced by sending it to the courts, one would think that the same board consisting of competent people would not send a case to court if it felt it was not in the best interests of the case.
I do not understand why the Minister does not want to give his own board the power to refer a particular situation to a court of law. Perhaps he could explain because, with all due respect to the Minister, he has not adequately explained why he does not want to give his own board the power to refer a particular case to a court when it feels it is absolutely necessary or appropriate under the circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a couple of points on the same issue. Many of the provinces hope that when this Bill is passed and the debt review panel is in place they will not have to implement or develop other legislation that would give the kind of protection to the farmers they hope this Act will provide. It ran out in 1985 and was extended for one year. It runs out again at the end of this year, but the Government has the authority to extend it. Had this particular clause been in place, this referral to courts, I think it might have been able to let it die. It will not be able to do so under the circumstances of this particular Act. I wonder what the Government of Ontario will have to do if, after the Act is passed, it finds that it does not have the kind of teeth that were promised and were to be, it was hoped, part of the Act.
On March 6, 1986, the Minister, in answer to a question by me, promised that the Government would be bringing forth debt review legislation as quickly as possible. When I suggested that it would not have any teeth, he said, "There will be teeth in it. Just wait and see". Now the teeth are what he is pulling out or refusing to put in at this time.
Mr. Chairman, we are not speaking of write-downs in this particular situation. That is not the issue. The Minister, should he let this clause go through to become part of the Act, would still have the authority of writing the regulations to define exactly what the court would review. If he is worried about the problem of write downs, which the banks and some of the financial institutions have indicated, then that could be part of the regulations. However, when there are injustices and when the voluntary agreements are not forthcoming, and the panel has recognized that the voluntary agreement which it intended or tried to impose or put in place is not forthcoming, then it should have the authority to refer that matter to a court of proper jurisdiction and, consequently, give it the opportunity to be settled by a third party or fourth party, as in this case. A second stage will then be available. That is exactly the position that has been taken by a couple of organizations. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture very specifically suggests that the court should be in the process.

In reviewing the proposals for changes in the Bankruptcy Act, we have a series of four options suggested for farmers and fishermen. Two of those options indicate need and the suggestion that a court be placed in the structure for a last level of decision-making, for an overview by someone who has not been involved. It suggests that both the borrower and the lender have the authority or the alternative to refer it to the court. In what is being suggested in this amendment, the people who would refer it to the court would be the panel, the group that has been adjudicating it all along. Out of the four options suggested in the changes to the Bankruptcy Act, two include court procedures, and the one recommended by the committee is definitely a court procedure, as well. Therefore, I do not think that we are suggesting that the Minister put in place something that will get a negative reaction from the financial community, but, rather, something which would allow him to know satisfactorily that there is always a place of appeal for the panel if the creditor, or the farmer, sits back and refuses to co-operate. In most cases, I would imagine it would be the creditor, because the farmer would be there because of difficulty.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that we do not spend all of our time dealing with this particular clause, because I know that we can make rapid progress on those remaining, and we must revert back to two or three earlier clauses, on which we have already agreed. I do not know what more I can say on this issue except to say that the message is loud and clear. It is a very important section, a very important issue. It is very sensitive out there. We know what the provincial reaction will be. We know what the majority of individual farmers feel about this and, probably, most of the commodity organizations. Indeed, this amendment has triggered a number of representations to our office. We held a debriefing meeting for the farm leaders yesterday, here in Ottawa. They met the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, myself and others in Vancouver, and most of them took the time to come to me yesterday. Most of them were from western Canada. They said, in fact, that we should proceed on the basis of the way in which we are proceeding here. They are very cautious at this time in extending additional powers. It is true that we could amend it. However, our difficulty here is that, as I am told, we cannot set the terms of reference for the courts under regulation. There is some question as to just how, in what detail, one could even establish the actions of the court in legislation. If one looks at the amendment here, a court of competent jurisdiction is to formulate the arrangement that it deems equitable under the circumstance.
I say to the Hon. Member for Prince Albert that the legislation, in my opinion, particularly with the review process that we are attaching to it, will be as effective as the Saskatchewan legislation. The only input the court would have in Saskatchewan would be that it would have the power not to formulate arrangements but, rather, to delay, as I understand it.

I ask for co-operation again to see if we cannot set this clause aside and move forward, make progress. We can get this behind us and we can be provided with an opportunity to work, in the next four to six weeks, to get it in place and allow it to operate. We can come back and review the progress at the earliest time that we have something to review. Therefore, I ask Hon. Members' co-operation in moving along with other clauses.

Mr. Chairman, I want to be very brief and make only one or two quick remarks. Like the Minister, I would like the Bill to go through as quickly as possible. The Minister said something to the effect that we were very limited in what we could do, either by regulation or even, in some cases, by legislation, in so far as directions that we could give to the court are concerned. However, I want to remind Members that what we are asking in this clause is not that at all. We do not want to prescribe how the court will adjudicate the case. We only want to prescribe to the board the authority to refer it to the court. I am sure that the court can deal with this afterwards in whatever way it desires. I just wish to establish the difference for the Minister.

I would also like to offer the Minister a possible further amendment which may satisfy this point. I will put it forward informally for the time being and send a copy of it out in writing to the Minister sometime later. I suggest that after the word "delay" in the third sentence, the following words should be added: "after satisfying the conditions set out in the regulations". It could then set out under what circumstances the board would be able to refer the matter to the court. In other words, the board would have to be satisfied that there has been an injustice or an undue delay, as well as meeting whatever other requirements the Minister puts into regulation. In this way the Minister can make the regulations very tight if he so chooses, giving a small amount of latitude to the board to refer matters to the court. If the board requests that the Minister give it further latitude, because of situations in which it sees that it would require authority, the Minister could then loosen up some of the regulations giving additional power to the board instead of having to come back to the House and ask for a further amendment in order to do just that.
The amendment could be in the form which I have just advocated. Perhaps the Minister's officials could word it in such a way as to ensure that it would do what it is intended to do. In other words, we are trying to give more latitude to the Minister to make it as strict as he likes in order to fulfil that condition, but only so that the board can have that power when required.
I have consulted my colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma with respect to this particular amendment. He is of the view, as am I, that it would further enhance the Bill. It is a watered-down version of his clause, but we believe it is a compromise with which the Minister could live. After all, he is the one who will have the final authority in terms of making
the regulation. He can make it as severe or as loose as he feels is appropriate in order to allow the board to make a reference to the court under whatever conditions are prescribed in the regulations.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know that I have anything more to add in response to the Hon. Member's advice than what I have already put forward. I have the clear sense that the issue is so sensitive that it is impossible for us to move on it at this time. I will tell the Hon. Member that if he wants to give me some latitude and do something for the farmers who will be taking advantage of this legislation, then let us move it along.
I wish to leave with the Hon. Member the message that I am not ruling this matter out forever. I think it is very important. It is also very sensitive and complex. The appropriate time for its consideration would be at the time of the review process. However, I must reject it now for all types of reasons. We will undertake to consider that aspect because, indeed, it will be the main focal point when we do the review.

Mr. Chairman, I have two or three brief questions which I wish to ask of the Minister, who has worked with members of both opposition Parties assiduously and effectively to take care of most of the problem areas that we have with the Bill, with the exception of the area dealing with the courts. We heard his arguments in private yesterday, and previously, when we were attempting to redraft clauses of the Bill. I have three short questions which, if answered, would clearly set out the Minister's position.
My understanding is that at this time the Minister does not have the authority of Cabinet to permit this type of a motion. Will the Minister admit that in fact the proposal is consistent with the bankruptcy procedure being proposed by the review committee which studied this area of the law? Is it not in fact the procedure which it recommends we follow, namely, that as a last resort there be a reference to the court?
The Minister seemed to convey in one of his previous responses this afternoon that there is some concern with respect to the way the court authority will be perceived by the provinces. I am not sure I quite understand that position. Will the Minister clarify it? It seems to me that the courts in this country have always been perceived, and I think correctly, as agencies of justice which generally act on behalf of property. Since that is the generally recognized assessment of what the courts do in this country, is the Minister concerned that the courts might rule on the side of the farmer more often than on the side of the banks? Is that the problem?
My third question has to do with provincial jurisdiction. We all know that the provinces still have constitutional authority with respect to property rights and land. My Party has always defended that position. We think that is where property rights ought to remain. Given that the courts are seen as the protectors of property and generally come down on its side, I really cannot understand why the provinces would be opposed to having the board refer certain cases to a court on certain
June 26, 1986

limited occasions. The provinces have jurisdiction over the land, and the courts generally favour the landed. What is the problem in terms of the provinces with respect to this rather minor, although important, amendment which would give the farmer one last attempt to have his case looked at and adjudicated by a court?
In our system of jurisprudence and in our system of Government the court is deemed to be the place where one can go when one feels that an injustice has been done. That is all this motion is concerned with. It is quite clear that it is concerned only with cases where an injustice appears to have been done and the board would then have the authority to refer.
Will the Minister very clearly spell out what the problem is since this recommendation is consistent with the bankruptcy procedure being proposed by the committee which is studying the issue? It is a recommendation that is preferred by the committee. Why is the Minister afraid of letting the matter go to the courts, in light of the fact that the courts generally favour property? What is the problem in terms of the provinces since they are responsible for property? They would simply come out as the winners in terms of this particular amendment.

Mr. Chairman, in response to the Hon. Member's questions I think there is the real possibility that if we accept this amendment then we will violate the record of decision. Because of the sensitivity involved in this respect every party and every group involved in this lengthy process from start to finish was only interested in clarification of one thing. That one thing was: Is there any legislative authority carried in this legislation which will in any way extend power to the courts or a review panel? When the question was answered negatively everyone was on our side. We went through all the steps in considering this proposal. They were quite complicated since they involve a couple of other Government Departments, and we had very close consultations with our provincial counterparts.
I would now like to move to the matter of the provinces. As Hon. Members know, flowing from the First Ministers' Conference the Prime Minister and the provincial Premiers assigned the Ministers of Agriculture the task of establishing working task forces on four or five subjects. Those task forces have been in motion and have been working hard and diligently on those special areas since January. I met with my provincial counterparts and have talked with them on a daily basis. We met specifically on two occasions, the first time in January and the next in March. As the Hon. Member can appreciate, the time we spent on farm finance occupied probably as much time as the time we spent on all of the other subjects put together.
At the January meeting, I wanted to make it very, very clear. I wanted to explain to my counterparts exactly where we were coming from on this piece of legislation. I wanted no
Farm Debt Review Act
mistake made and wanted to know exactly where they were going to stand. I told them that we would not move to the next item on the agenda until I knew exactly where they were coming from.
Representatives from eight of the provinces told me with no uncertainty that they would accept the route we were going. There was no way that they would have any part of a piece of legislation which extended the power of a write-down to a court or a review panel. The two provincial representatives who said they would accept that with some conditions were from the Province of Manitoba and the Province of Newfoundland. That is the score on that question.
Regarding the advisory recommendations, as Hon. Members will know, Ministers have advisory groups, boards or commissions for a great many purposes and they perform a very useful service. The advisory group to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on the Bankruptcy Act did a very useful job. A very competent individual looked at the question from an agricultural point of view and the group brought forward a recommendation.
Hon. Members will know that as a Government, we have an obligation and responsibility to study those recommendations. If we think certain recommendations are good, we accept them. Sometimes we think that others might be good as well but perhaps the timing is wrong. To answer the question, we have not accepted all of the recommendations.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the Minister of Agriculture talk about the reactions of the various provinces. The day he introduced this legislation a few weeks ago, the Saskatchewan Minister of Agriculture, when asked what he thought of the legislation, indicated that he would be examining it and if he did not find it comprehensive enough, he would stick with his own legislation. Clearly his own legislation is much more comprehensive. Under Saskatchewan law, if a deadlock occurs a review board prepares a recommendation which is sent to the court and must be given more weight than in any other province.
I would ask the Minister to recall that when he met with the Minister of Agriculture for Prince Edward Island, he pointed out to him that the banks have incredible powers and are able to put incredible pressures on farmers. For instance, many people who have worked on review boards have suggested to me that the banks often tell farmers, when their notes are due, that if they want their notes extended, the only way that can be done is by putting them on a floating rate.
There are all kinds of injustices which have become apparent to members of these review panels. Not only will they be powerless to recommend to the review board of the province that the matter be sent to a court but they will be powerless to speak of what is going on outside the panel. There is a double whammy there. A great many farmers are concerned about that.
We know that there is going to be a drastic and almost cataclysmic restructuring of farm debt for at least 8,000 or

June 26, 1986
Farm Debt Review Act
maybe 10,000 farmers or more in the next few years. Yet there is a danger that a farmer can go into the review process but get no satisfaction because the board has no power and cannot do anything when the process is over because that would contravene a clause of this Bill about communicating anything that was said or done within the review panel. It is rather like a star chamber. The farmer goes to the panel, makes his pitch and the banks sit on their hands for 60, 90 or 120 days. Then everyone is sworn to secrecy. Then the Minister's $50-million program for farm adjustment comes in, the farmer is hustled off his farm and the bank gets the farm. The farmer is out of farming probably for the rest of his life.
When the Minister said that he had across-the-board support from all provinces, he may have thought that that is what he had. It certainly does not appear to be the case from what the Minister of Agriculture for Saskatchewan has said and it certainly does not jibe with what the Minister of Agriculture for Prince Edward Island told me.
I would suggest to the Minister that he only turn to the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey who is assisting him this afternoon to ask about what was found out in the Bruce-Grey pilot project. Those people found out that the banks made no decisions and waited out the time. After the review process was over, the banks foreclosed and did not make a very serious attempt to reach an agreement.
This amendment in the way it is drafted is not dealing with a court order or restructuring of debt. All it deals with is cases of injustice or undue delay. I would like to see a banker come before this committee this afternoon to say that he wants to be able to be unjust to a farmer who has fallen on hard times and does not want the board to have the right to refer that to a court of justice for the formulation of an arrangement that it deems equitable under the circumstances. It seems to me that there are very few bankers who are hard hearted enough to put that proposition before the committee this afternoon.
The Minister indicated that he agreed to the amendment to Clause 38 or Clause 39 provided that the entire question is referred to a committee of the House. I assume it would be the Agriculture Committee or a subcommittee of that committee. If that committee is to be struck and established next January, it might review the situation and find that this kind of amendment or something equivalent to it might be appropriate. Would the Minister give an undertaking to the House that he will seek support for such an amendment and bring it before the House, assuming that the committee that will review this Act makes such a recommendation? The Minister has already spoken several times about the idea of the review that is being proposed. I wonder if he would be willing to do that, because clearly farm organizations have been asking for this kind of legislation for some time.
Four or five years ago, I believe, the Minister served on a committee of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, and legislation much stronger than this was before the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee of the House in June 1984. Legislation much stronger but similar in nature to this
legislation was put before that committee two years ago. It is little wonder, since the Minister promised this legislation last July 10, that everyone was amazed that he did not get around to bringing the legislation before the House until mid-June.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the National Farmers Union, the wheat pools, and so on support the amendment which I have put forward. Could the Minister indicate whether he would be prepared to bring in an appropriate amendment, if it is recommended by the standing committee when it reviews the legislation next January or at the beginning of next year?

Mr. Chairman, I want to set the record straight. I indicated that I met with my provincial counterparts in January and March. I said that two provinces would accept mandatory write-downs. Since that time there has been a change in the Government of P.E.I.
A change for the better.
In fact, I think it has some good sense as far as its approach to review legislation is concerned. It recently set up a review panel with no legal power.
Absolutely no power at all.

That is correct. The new Government of P.E.I. is just as aware of the situation. It demonstrates understanding, appreciation, and the caution which must be exercised at this time when dealing with the issue.
The Hon. Member asked me to give a commitment now. It would be irresponsible for me to do so, not having the track record of the review boards and not having the advice of the standing committee. Who knows? More than likely the Hon. Member will be a member of the committee. I am sure he would want the committee to have the opportunity to hear witnesses. I would be anxious to receive his recommendations at that time, which I think is the only appropriate time.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister keeps suggesting that he will have the track record of the review boards before us. Unfortunately, the recommendations which might force us to make a change in the Act will have gone down the drain as far as farmers are concerned. They will not have had an extra chance.
We suggest that the Minister should include this clause now so that farmers would be given some protection rather than wait for more examples of disaster. I realize that how disasters happen might result in changes. However, farmers will not be given a second chance. In effect, the Government is condemning the first group of people who appear before these panels to being examples of how the legislation should be changed. I think we should include something to safeguard against that.

Mr. Chairman, in his comments a couple of minutes ago, the Minister suggested that the people with
June 26, 1986

whom he discussed the matter wanted to be sure that review boards had absolutely no powers with regard to restructuring debt. If there are to be absolutely no powers with regard to restructuring debt, how does the Minister expect the whole system to function? Clearly that was the problem with the Grey-Bruce pilot project. It dealt with some 25 or 26 applications out of a total of approximately 90. Another problem was that the bankers sat on their hands. The FCC would not restructure their debt. The whole system stalled. Members of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and other representatives worked very hard, but there was no power of persuasion. In this piece of legislation there are no powers of persuasion. I believe that in Saskatchewan they have the power to refer the matter to a court and to recommend loan guarantees; they have some tools with which to work.
I would be interested in knowing just how the Minister expects the system to work since he said that he does not want any powers for the review panels. Obviously we are dealing with thousands of farmers. The value of their properties has dropped by as much as a third or two-thirds. There will be a drastic restructuring of debt. How does the Minister see the boards having the power to carry out this restructuring of debt when they do not have any more power than that of the Grey-Bruce pilot project and less power than that of the Saskatchewan review panels?

Mr. Chairman, I do not know why anyone would want to be so pessimistic or so negative. We have talked about the process for a long time. The provinces want to move in this direction. Farm organizations want to move in this direction. The majority of farmers want to move in this direction. We know that write-downs are going on all across the country. The problem is that it is happening in St. Thomas but not in Aylmer, which is some 12 miles away. There are many inequities. It is happening in one region and not in the other; it is happening in one province and not in the other. It is a very inequitable situation. We want to put some fairness and equity into the system across the country so that regardless of where farmers live, farm, or operate, and regardless of what banks they do business with, at least there are review panels and review boards to assist on their behalf.
I have confidence in the people who will be appointed to these boards. I am encouraged by the reaction of the banking community. We cannot shut them out. We cannot throw stones at them. We need them; we need the banks. To be safe, 75 per cent of farmers are not in a financial situation to use this. The Hon. Member should not think that they are not watching us right now. Their continued success relies very heavily on access to credit from conventional lending institutions.
The other people who are watching us very closely are those farmers who are reaching retirement. It is normal for a farmer to sell his farm and take back a mortgage. That is all he has; it is his pension plan. If we extend the power of a court to write down, those farmers will sell the property but they will do so without taking back mortgages and risking their pension plans.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister knows how the system works. Anyone who appears before or serves on a panel will be sworn to secrecy. That is in the Act. What happens when panel members become aware of an injustice, for example, where a bank has deliberately switched a farmer from a flat interest rate to a floating one and charged it for three years or four years? Everyone is sworn to secrecy, so how can such an injustice be redressed? The board is sworn to secrecy, as are farmers. How does the Minister see an injustice being handled? How does the farmer get assistance or redress if the review panel cannot refer the matter to the review board and to a proper court of justice?

Mr. Chairman, the best way I can answer the Hon. Member's first question is for him to give me an example. My understanding is that this would not happen, you just cannot do it. Second, the farmer is not sworn to secrecy, creditors are not sworn to secrecy. It is only the panel members who are.

Mr. Chairman, I would point out that Clause 36(1) states:
Except as authorized by subsection (2), no person shall knowingly communicate or knowingly allow to be communited to any person any information obtained from a farmer or from any creditor of a farmer under this Act or knowingly allow any person to inspect or have access to any such information.
It is my information that members of the panel are sworn to secrecy. They cannot blow the whistle, so to speak, on a lending institution which has taken part in an improper or an unjust Act against the farmer.

Member for Algoma correctly pointed out that it was necessary to have a review process since the impending suspension of the sitting has made it impossible to hear from the banks, farm organizations and others who might be affected by the legislation. be proposed. We think this might provide some moral authority to remind both the lender and others involved in the process that their actions will be reviewed and the results or lack thereof will be considered and new legislation may be proposed as a result.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if we can get a commitment from the Minister that the Act will come into force in 1986 and that it would be his intention to have the matter referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture. The clause does not make it clear. It says "any committee so designated". As I read this, it would take a House order to refer it to the committee. It also says that it comes into force in the calendar year in which the Act comes into force. I assume that it is going to be 1986, but I want a commitment from the Minister that that is when it will happen.

Mr. Chairman, the short answer is yes, 1986. I do not know whether I can say it would be the Standing Committee on Agriculture or not, but obviously that seems to be the appropriate standing committee.

I have to confess to having been party to the vagueness of the wording. Mr. Chairman, you will recall that on Friday we stood four clauses, those being Clauses 17, 18, 19 and 20. I think we are now in a position, are we not, to go back and deal with them? I proposed this last Friday when we were in Committee of the Whole. I think a Bill like this, which is designed to assist farmers in their worst financial crisis in 50 years, could involve a very intimidating situation if the farmer were to receive suddenly a note from his friendly farm debt review board that his chartered bank had just moved to have him reviewed. At the same time he would have to give his consent under the existing clauses in the Bill. Yet what choice does he have? With this clause removed, had we succeeded in getting an amendment so that where an injustice was done to a farmer the matter could be referred to a court, we could have been pretty sure that this whole procedure would not become one to silence farmers and quietly hustle them off their land. Mr. Chairman, I was pointing out that the way the Bill is drafted it might create major problems concerning the administration of public funds in Quebec.
I pointed out that in 1984-85 the Farm Credit Bureau had dealt with close to 9,500 applications for long- and mid-term loans, whereas the federal Farm Credit Corporation made fewer than 100 loans. A few more loans were made at the federal level in 1985-86, but most such loans came from the Quebec Farm Credit Bureau.
Given the way the review panels are established under the legislation, to a certain extent an organization created by the federal Government will administer public funds allocated by another Parliament. In other words a farm loan made-indeed since the legislation covers ... Clause 3 states that:
This Act is binding on Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province.
This means that people sitting on the review panel-I am sure the Minister will appoint qualified people-will have to make decisions concerning funds allocated by another Parliament where various organizations must report to the Quebec National Assembly.
I wanted to go on record and point out the difficulties involved with respect to the administration and the way public funds are administered, and the responsibilities given to each level of government. The situation in Quebec is particular in the sense that the Farm Credit Bureau has a role to play, much like the federal Farm Credit Corporation.
I think the Minister should have provided that when review panels are set up for loans made by an agency of a provincial government or a provincial legislative assembly, that on these review panels provided in the clauses we are now adopting or debating, with amendments, we have representatives duly appointed by the people and the administrative bodies that are responsible for administering these funds.
When the provisions of this legislation are put in effect, we can expect a considerable rise in the cost of Government administration, especially for the Office du credit agricole, because in some cases they will have to postpone carrying out their mandate for as many as 90 or 120 days, and this will result in a considerable loss of interest and high administration costs.
I would like to ask the Minister whether he has considered these problems and whether he would be able to inform the House-I realize he really wants this Bill to be passed. I also

realize that it is important for Canadians across the country and that we must find a solution to this problem. However, could the Minister perhaps inform the House and give it the assurance that the study that will be carried out, pursuant to the clause we adopted earlier, which will be an argument in favour of revising certain clauses of the Bill-that we will have a chance to put the membership of these panels on a broader basis and that the Quebec Legislative Assembly will be responsible for appointing at least some of the members of the review boards, since these are public funds approved by another parliament?
And second, could the Minister give the House the assurance that, together with his Quebec counterpart and Quebec officials, he will look into the possibility of signing a federal-provincial agreement to deal with this problem? It is a problem which I think is very important, since in Quebec, most farm loans, whether long, medium or short term, are not granted by the federal authorities but by a provincial agency which is called the Office du credit agricole. Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the Hon. Member's comments and observations regarding being very, very cautious about putting into law something here in the House of Commons that would unilaterally decree on the duly elected provincial legislature of any province. I suggest that the Hon. Member talk with his colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma.
I did talk to him.

When I was responding to question after question after question about what the provincial reaction would be, the province said no. It is fine, go along with what you suggest to us, but do not extend the power of a court or a review board to unilaterally write down debt. That is why.
That is not what I am asking.

Just a minute. Quebec is not paying the cost of the review panels. Ontario is not carrying the cost of that, the federal Government is. We are carrying that.
I do not know if the Member was here throughout the day or last Friday, but if we have a ten-man panel, I have invited our provincial colleagues to submit three names to us. That is a reasonable number to expect from a provincial Government. In addition, I said last Friday that there was an open invitation to all Members of this House to supply us with a list of names of those who would serve on review panels and also on review boards.
If the province does not want to participate as a creditor in a write down, like any other creditor, then there is no legal obligation to do so. I want to tell you that they are very, very sensitive about that.

The Minister failed to grasp what I meant. What I am trying to say is that the funds involved where the Office du credit agricole is concerned are not private funds. These are funds that were approved by a Parliament that happens to be the Parliament of Quebec, but it could just as well have been the Parliament of Ontario, if there is one in Ontario, but I know that is how things are done in Quebec. These funds are managed, and the Office du credit agricole must report to the National Assembly, just as here we have parliamentary committees that meet and are supposed to report back to the House. In this particular case, a body that approves funds at the provincial level would be subject to control by a federal system, without there being any participation involved. As far as I know, there has been no federal-provincial agreement on the subject, at least for... I don't know about the other provinces, but I am referring to Quebec.
I was not referring to the cost of the system itself but to the cost that would be incurred by the Office du credit agricole in complying with this request. And suppose we take, I don't know ... How many are there? Maybe 10 per cent, 5 per cent or 8 per cent of these loans. If a 100 or 125 cases are submitted for review, obviously some very high costs will be incurred, not only by the Financial institutions, in the case of private institutions that's one thing, but in the case of public institutions, there are certain regulations, and these costs, I don't know how to assess them, but if we say 5 per cent or 10 per cent, this is going to mean an enormous amount in terms of lost interest. And also in terms of additional staff requirements.
I am rather surprised that without prior federal-provincial agreement this Bill should be introduced not only to impose additional costs to the Quebec Farm Credit Bureau and to the National Assembly, but also to create a problem with respect to responsibility for expenditures by a legislative assembly which approved them and the federal Parliament which adopts legislation and tells a group which it has created: You have the mandate. This is not legally binding, of course, but it still amounts to strong pressure.
I have a question for the Minister, for I realize that we cannot expect at this stage-the Bill is to be adopted in the next few minutes-to have the file re-opened with a view to securing a federal-provincial agreement. But I did suggest and ask him to hold discussions with his colleague or with Quebec Credit agricole authorities so see what kind of problems will be created by the administration of this Act and perhaps make the appropriate changes in the future.

Mr. Chairman, we have had close and continuing consultations with provincial counterparts in the past on this and other matters. We will continue to do so, particularly at the wish of the Hon. Member.
