subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE BUDGET ADVISABILITY OF REDUCING NATIONAL DEBT

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Attewell (Don Valley East) moved:
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE BUDGET ADVISABILITY OF REDUCING NATIONAL DEBT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to require the government to present an annual budget in which total annual outlays do not exceed total annual receipts and such total receipts will exclude those derived from borrowing and total outlays will exclude those for interest costs on the national debt and for repayment of the debt principal.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is really quite an honour to speak tonight on this Private Member's Motion of mine, M-86. It was first placed on the Order Paper on December 20, 1985. In the few minutes allotted to me, I want to speak briefly of the background and gravity of this problem, of Canada's record in terms of deficits, the ever increasing national debt of this country, of our Government's achievements so far to turn the situation around and what some other countries are doing, for instance, the United States of America, and then summarize my thoughts and views on the subject. I think we must all attach extreme gravity to the situation. Indeed, we must come to realistic grips with this ever-widening gap of spending compared to what we have been taking in.
I have had numerous discussions with my constituents in Don Valley East and, almost to a person, they are supportive of this type of resolution. Let me just make a few points, because the problem is not unique to Canada. I think it is accurate to say that all levels of government have overspent. Taxpayers are simply fed up and frustrated with the track record, if I could put it that way, of a number of politicians around this world in terms of the lack of prudent thinking and lack of restraint in the spending of their precious tax dollars.
National Debt
For longer than most voters and most western democracies can remember, one of life's certainties has been the reckless spending by so many governments. Government spending has been increasing for too long as a percentage of Gross National Product. In 1960, for instance, only two countries belonging to the OECD had spending in excess of one-third of their Gross National Product. However, 25 years later, in 1985, 23 out of 24 countries in that organization were spending in excess of one-third of their GNP. In fact, the average was 45 per cent, and it varied from 31 per cent in Switzerland to 64 per cent in Sweden.
Let us examine Canada's record in that respect, and I will return to the last year in which we could boast of a surplus, the year 1969-70, when a surplus of $331 million was recorded. Let me just highlight the fact that the total national debt at that time was slightly under $18 billion. In 1971-72, we went through the $1 billion annual deficit figure, hitting $1.5 billion. In 1975-76, we went through the $5 billion figure, hitting $5.7 billion. In 1977-78, we soared through the $10 billion annual deficit level, and by that time our national debt had climbed to $48.3 billion. In 1982-83, we hit $27.6 billion. In 1983-84, we went through the $30 billion level at $32.4 billion. In 1984-85, a projection was some $38.2 billion, which would have been the case if, indeed, the Government had not changed hands and the Conservative Government had not taken some extreme action which I will recapitulate in a few moments.
It is interesting to point out that if one follows that track record of excessive spending well beyond our means for over a decade, one finds there is a correlation between that and the drop of our Canadian dollar. When that overspending started a decade or so ago, our dollar was something like $1.05 versus the U.S. dollar, and it has slid, year by year, to a level now of some 72 cents. The interest cost now totals some $24 billion or $25 billion a year to service the massive national debt of some $220 billion or $230 billion. That interest cost now, on an annual basis, amounts to $1,024 for every man, woman and child in this country of Canada.
Our spending, as a percentage of GNP, was some 16.6 per cent in 1974-75, at the start of our real problem, and it soared to 45 per cent in 1984-85. Had we let the status quo remain intact, and had this spending pattern continued, we project it would have reached an alarming level of 63 per cent of GNP by 1990-91; but, indeed, the Government has taken several major initiatives to try to turn the situation around.
In November of 1984, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) made a very comprehensive economic statement of what was to happen over the next few years, and some savings of $4 billion were identified at that time. The Budget in May of 1985 was another landmark in the direction of fiscal restraint, and it was followed by the Budget of February 26, 1986, when again, the annual deficit was forecast to decrease below the $30 billion level. Discretionary spending was decreased to under 3 per cent. Then, of course, another major initiative came to the reporting stage just a few months ago. I refer to the Nielsen



June 26, 1986
National Debt
task force. I believe some 989 projects of the Government were reviewed in great detail by a number of private sector people and others. Many people, including myself, are expecting great savings of taxpayers' dollars when the individual committees consider the various options and recommendations within the group.
Let me summarize. By now, most people have heard of the Gramm-Rudman-Hollings Bill in the United States. It was signed into law by President Reagan on December 12, 1985. It is calling for a balanced Budget by 1991. There are some exceptions, but it is basically now taking it out of the politicians' hands because of the pattern that we have seen, because of the lack of discipline that has been enjoyed, and it is putting it in the hands of a mechanism which triggers cuts to be made in defence and other areas if these predescribed levels of spending are not met.
I do believe what our Government has achieved since September, 1984, is of real significance, but it is a mammoth task. Concerning almost every issue we touch, one witnesses kicking and screaming and objections from the other side of the House. This has been the case whether involving transfer payments that we were proposing to increase from $65 billion to $90 billion over the next few years, or involving other areas, because society is so organized these days in terms of constituency groups. Therefore, it is difficult indeed to cut back. I happen to think, as much as I regret saying it, that we need that type of mechanism in this country, literally taking a fair amount of the decision out of the politicians' hands and putting it into legislation. If we just think back into our own lives, and through reading history, we realize that one of the paramount virtues voters expected of their parliamentarians was prudent, careful, conscious, deliberate action in terms of the spending of those precious tax dollars.
I do not think we can be proud in this country, thanks largely to the record that was set up by the previous Government, of what has happened. It is now too large to turn around in a discretionary way. I would urge my colleagues on both sides of the House to vote "yes" when this particular motion comes to that vote. I am honoured that this particular motion is the first Private Members' Motion under parliamentary reform to be chosen for voting. In other words, it will receive up to five hours of debate. It is certainly worthy of that type of earnest debate so that Canadians can become more aware of the real gravity of the situation and why, indeed, it needs legislative action to turn it around and to brighten that outlook and future for Canadians so that we will have some manoeuvrability involving much-needed social programs, whether in health care or education.
We owe it not only to our children but to our grandchildren to turn this around in a meaningful way. I predict that if we can do this, it will be one of the most difficult but rewarding tasks we undertake, not only of the last 25 years but of the last century. It is of that gravity.
I hope to be speaking to this Bill again. However, if it does come to a votable situation shortly, I hope that all Members will join with me in voting in favour of having it referred to a committee where it will receive extensive deliberation. Several weeks ago I visited Senator Gramm in his office in Washington. He is an economist who worked on the details of his Bill, in conjunction with his other colleagues, for over four years. I know that in a few hours we will not be able to put together in this House, or in committee, anything of that nature, because it is a very complex situation. However, we should not let the complexity of it stand in the way of solving this most serious problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege to rise tonight to add my views to the debate on this interesting issue. I have a great deal of respect and admiration for my hon. friend who has introduced this motion. However, I suspect this is where we depart on some philosophical differences.
It is appropriate to remind Hon. Members that there was really only one Government in Canada that for many years balanced its books. It was a Government which felt that running a fiscally-responsible Government was appropriate. While it inherited a mess left by past Liberal Governments, it said: "We think it is useful that after we care for the needs of the people in our province and provide the necessary support and stimulus to the sectors of the economy that we attempt to balance our books". That Government did that year after year and, in a sense, decade after decade. I refer to the Government of Tommy Douglas of the Province of Saskatchewan, a CCF and New Democratic Government. I say that it was the only Government in Canada that for years and years was debt-free.
I wish to place that on the record so that we can understand the partisan importance of this particular motion.
I also wish to remind my hon. friend that the biggest proponent of this particular initiative is President Reagan. We do not necessarily want to accept what the President says. However, more important, we do not want to see what he does. If we were to add up all of the deficits in the United States over the last 200 years, including the deficit which came out of the Civil War, the First World War, the Second World War, the Korean War, and back to the Depression, we would see that the deficit of President Reagan in his eight years of administration will mount up to twice the accumulated United States deficit over the last 200 years. So when this individual says that he is concerned about the deficit and plans to take action against it, his actions betray exactly the opposite behaviour.
The motion of my colleague reflects a view of Government in which people see Government as something based on the same principles as the Chrysler Corporation. Their point of view is that Government ought to be run as a corporation is run, with success or failure being determined on the basis of quarterly balance sheets. In other words this motion says that if a Government can balance its books, then it is a good Government. In my estimation, that really misses the point.
June 26, 1986

Government is not a private profit-maximizing institution. In fact, it has the responsibility to maintain general economic and socially favourable conditions in a country. In many cases a Government has the duty to intervene in the economy if such an initiative will encourage economic growth and prosperity.
This is a very hard lesson for Canada and other countries to learn. It was born out of the experiences of the Great Depression. At that time the traditional laissez-faire economics which prevailed suggested that when there was an economic downturn, government spending should be cut back. At that time it was thought that the duty of Government was to reduce its spending to match the reduced revenues which come in during difficult economic times. We saw that as the Depression persisted, unemployment rose and economic and social conditions worsened.
It was in 1936 that John Maynard Keynes wrote his General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. In it he proposed that left to itself, the market economy would settle into permanent recession or depression. He proposed that the State pick up the slack and run a deficit where necessary to inject the needed purchasing power into the economy. President Roosevelt of the United States listened carefully to what Keynes had to say. In a sense Roosevelt followed many of Keynes' theories in terms of his initiatives and the economy of the United States started to turn around. The country of Sweden listened to Mr. Keynes and applied many of his theories prior to those written in 1936. As a result the depression in Sweden was relatively minimal. The conditions in that country were not as oppressive as they were in most other western industrialized nations.
The biggest Keynesian experiment was World War II when the Government had to borrow massively to finance the war effort. Consequently, the economy boomed and unemployment fell dramatically. The question I would put to my hon. friend is this. Would he have advocated in such circumstances that the Government not borrow to invest in the productive capacity to win the war in this case?
The post World War II era shows us that successive Governments have used short-term deficit spending to combat periodic bouts of unemployment and depressed economic conditions. However, in 1975 the government began experiencing consistent budget deficits. Why was this? I suggest that since 1975 the economy grew more slowly. As a result, more payments were required in the form of unemployment insurance and welfare. Of course, fewer revenues came into the federal government coffers as a result of taxes paid that would reflect a strong economy when exactly the reverse was happening. There were difficult economic times which resulted in fewer taxes.
As a result, at this time the federal Government introduced a wide-ranging set of tax expenditures. I call them tax loopholes for generalized descriptive purposes. In 1983 Mr. Lalonde said in his Budget: "The increased federal deficit over the second half of the 1970s was not due to runaway expenditure growth. It was due in large part to a succession of tax cuts
National Debt
introduced in response to weak economic activity". On a number of occasions the Economic Council of Canada has confirmed this eroding tax base and, consequently, fewer and fewer dollars come in as a result.
In my closing comments I wish to say that we are not suggesting that deficits are good. We are not suggesting that the present state of affairs in this country is not something about which to be very concerned. We have to be careful that we do not move ahead blindly, not recognizing the responsibility that we have as parliamentarians. The Government must accept the responsibility that when times are tough an investment might be required. After all, any good businessman knows that to make money one has to invest money.
In order to have a strong economy, we may have to invest a certain number of dollars in the development of transportation systems, ports, in assisting small business and farmers to get into new ventures and so on. In other words, there is a time for the Government to invest in a way that would result in economic prosperity and growth. Consequently, additional revenues through personal, sales, excise and corporate tax could be raised as a result to pay for that growth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank Hon. Members opposite and the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) for giving me an opportunity to speak on this important subject of gating. I want to begin in a more general way by looking at how we Canadians have the problem with which we are faced. We have to look at the question of gating within the context of security we seek for society.
People often forget that in Canada we are extremely fortunate because we do not have a high crime rate and we do not have a high rate of violent crime. We do, however, have a very high rate of punishment. We send a large number of people to prison compared to other countries, far more than western European countries and we send them to prison for very long periods of time. Part of this, I suspect, is the influence of television. Canadians think we have far more of a crime problem than we actually do and think we have far more violent crime than we actually do. People see so much in fictitious situations on television which is largely American television. It is perhaps an exaggeration for American society but it is even more of an exaggeration for our society. We have this context of fear with which people approach the subject.
We have people saying we need these new tough measures. They are not new tough measures. They are very old measures, measures of repression that we have got away from and instituted a rule of law which is better. Yet people think we need these extremely severe measures to deal with our crime problem, exaggerating the nature of that crime problem and the extent of violence in our own society. A number of extremely important organizations and experts on the subject have intervened and have given us the benefit of their advice. I would like to begin with the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies.
The Elizabeth Fry Society is well known for its work in the field of dealing with prisoners and for making recommendations to Government as to the design of a safe system for society and a humane system, one that achieves a reasonable balance. I happen to be a member of the Canadian Elizabeth Fry Society. I cannot say I am an active member but I support its work whole-heartedly. I want to quote from the brief it prepared to intervene on Bill C-67. It is strongly opposed to these measures:
"The measures proposed in Bill C-67 to protect society, however, are far too sweeping, offend principles of fundamental justice, and provide no assurance that violence will be reduced. The measures do not address the roots of the problem of
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
violence but rather, at best, are likely to more than delay future violence by a few prisoners, while unreasonably unjustly extending the loss of liberty of many.
That is a fundamental criticism of this Bill. It will result in some people remaining in prison for a longer period of time. However, not indefinitely. Let us not be under any illusion that this will lock up dangerous people, that the key will be turned and they will never get out again. Most prisoners are eventually released into society. This means people will be released after many years, not necessarily in any more fit state to be returned to society and not necessarily prisoners who might cause further violence.
There are no assurances this Bill will make any one Canadian any safer than we are without this legislation.
Let me turn to another criticism voiced by the Elizabeth Fry Societies:
Bill C-67 would give new powers to the Parole Board to place a detention order on certain prisoners until warrant expiry, or until the order is lifted. These powers will effectively change the role of the Parole Board to a detaining body, which we normally leave to courts which ensure due process, from that of a releasing body.
That is one of the fundamental objections which the NDP has to this Bill. It is giving powers to the Parole Board that ought properly to be exercised by a court of law with all of the protections for the accused in a court of law, a procedure that we have developed over the years. The next criticism reads:
The fact that the Parole Board would be able to use this detaining power in relation to anticipated rather than actual behaviour, based on criteria contained in Regulations which are themselves broad and which can be amended without parliamentary scrutiny, make the provision particularly offensive to existing traditions of due process within the Canadian criminal justice system. It is likely that the new provision will also be found to contravene Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
That is a very serious objection that has been raised, the possibility that the courts of our country, up to the Supreme Court of Canada, would find this legislation to be contrary to the Charter of Rights. There is a substantial reason for them so doing. The Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies is supportive in principle of the proposal that all prisoners be reviewed for conditional release by the date of day parole eligibility, as a way of accelerating the release of prisoners who do not pose a threat to society. I heartily endorse that recommendation as well. We are sending too many people to prison, people who are not risks to Canadian society. We keep them there at enormous expense. We do not provide more security for Canadians, but it costs taxpayers a great deal of money. The association's recommendation is a very eminently sensible one.
Also the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies has a number of objections to the proposed detention order. They relate to the arbitrary, illogical, and broad list of schedule offences to be used to identify prisoners who will automatically be considered for a detention order. The list is broad, and that is reason for the objection. Also they relate to the power to extend loss of liberty on the basis of a belief about future behaviour, predictions about which are not much better

June 26, 1986
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
than guesswork, rather than a court adjudicated criminal conviction.
This is one of the most serious objections to the legislation. This would mean people would spend time in prison, not on the basis of what they have done, which we agree is grounds for detaining people, but on the basis of a guess in terms of what they might do in the future. This is fundamentally contrary to our criminal justice system which has evolved over the years. That system includes a protection against this kind of abuse of power. This is a backward step. It is returning to abuses which we like to think we got away from.
Another objection relates to the absence of due process in the manner in which the review and decision will be made, such as lack of prior full disclosure of information to the prisoners, and inclusion of substantive matters in regulation rather than in law. Clearly there will not be full disclosure to prisoners. Of course there is a possibility that they will be detained on matters which are not subject to parliamentary scrutiny and can be changed without Parliament having anything to say about it. In fact they are very broad and very vague. This is entirely contrary to our notions of justice. People should be in prison only if they have violated a specific offence. Another specific objection relates to the erosion of the earned remission program and the principles upon which it is based.
What has happened is that we have very long sentences in Canada. In fact, they are becoming longer. One of the reasons sentences are so long is the provision for earned remission called "good time off'. Judges know that there is a possibility or a very likely probability that a prisoner will get this time off or a good proportion of it. Of course it is a carrot to the prisoner to be well behaved in prison because of the fear of loss of this good time. It is clearly an incentive to good behaviour. Judges know that prisoners will likely be getting out a substantial period before the end of the sentence ordered. As a result they make the sentence longer, expecting that a normal prisoner will have earned at least a substantial amount of that time off, if not all of it. Therefore, penalties are adjusted accordingly.
We have had this process, and we have seen sentences becoming longer. Here we have a provision which will keep people in prison for the period judges expected they would otherwise be out and gave them a longer sentence than would have been considered appropriate under the circumstances of the case.
Also the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies opposed the "one-chance" mandatory supervision provision whereby revoked prisoners who were originally convicted of a schedule offence, or one of the listed offences, would not be released again until the expiry of their warrant, thus losing existing and future remission. This means that these people will not have an incentive to good behaviour in that period. It also means making an extremely important decision at one point in time when the person might change subsequently. I think it suggests something very nasty about human nature. It suggests that we cannot have hope that people will change or
reform. Surely our society is based upon an understanding that people change and grow. That possibility should be allowed for. Instead what we have is the "one-chance" provision. If that chance is missed, no matter how much a person changes nor what experiences the person may have, he or she has missed it. It seems as if that is extremely arbitrary and reflects a very nasty understanding of human nature.
According to the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies, this appears to be a further sweeping, arbitrary, unfair measure, particularly given that it would be applied against prisoners revoked whether for the commission of a criminal offence or for a technical reason. We must understand that persons could lose their time under mandatory supervision, not because they committed a crime but because they violated some rule. This is blatantly unjust and cannot be supported, given the wide range of behaviour which could be involved. It could be a fairly trivial matter which caused the breach. It need not have been a serious matter.
Mandatory supervision has become a scapegoat for the crime problem in Canada. By focusing on an ever-restrictive mandatory supervision program, we continue to avoid the key questions which must be addressed if violent or dangerous crime is to be effectively combated. Human and financial resources must be directed toward relieving those conditions which create or contribute to the development of violent or dangerous people. That is the only way in which we will achieve any kind of security in society. It is not by longer and longer sentences for people who will eventually be released when their sentences come up. Very few people actually die of old age in prison; most people are eventually released. The way in which to achieve security is to attack violent and dangerous behaviour. For example, we have the need for stronger measures to deal with pornography and the need to get at the root of conditions which encourage violent behaviour.
These are the constructive things we can do. We are not helpless in the face of violent crime. There are many things which Parliament can do. There are many things which we as a society can do. However, they must be constructive things which get to the heart of the problem. We should not simply fool around with it to give an impression to the public that we care about security and that we are trying to do something in that regard, when in fact we are not, when in fact we will just build more prisons and lock up more people for longer periods of time. That will not solve the problem.
As well, the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies called for the abolition of mandatory supervision in the past because it believed that it undermined the purpose of earned remission and because supervision could only be effective if it was voluntary. It does not support this type of piecemeal, arbitrary demolition. The association wants a better system, not the backward step which the Bill before us proposes.
Over all we would hope that Parliament would not proceed with this legislative package because it cannot be expected to provide a genuine increase in the long-term safety of Canadian
June 26, 1986

society and will only exacerbate the misconceptions and problems which it purports to address. That is what is so very fundamentally wrong with the piece of legislation before us.
I have quoted fairly extensively from the excellent brief of the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies. I should like to add that the John Howard Society also made quite important and quite useful submissions on the same matter. The board of the John Howard Society of Kingston felt that it was important to offer its support to the accelerated release of low-risk inmates. It certainly felt that Canada incarcerated far too many people and for far too long. It also indicated that removing people from the community did little to improve their ability to function in the community. It supported efforts to provide real alternatives to incarceration.
This is what the people who know the most about the subject are telling us. They are telling us not to move in that direction. They are telling us to empty prisons of low-risk people and non-violent offenders. Also they are telling us to attack the real roots of the problem. Many experts have made the statement that these measures will not protect society. Underlying these measures is the presumption that we can predict who is likely to be dangerous. However, social science research and the experiences of the National Parole Board to date indicate that the ability to predict dangerousness is nonexistent. I am afraid that is all too true. Hundreds and hundreds of studies have shown that psychiatrists cannot predict, judges cannot predict, and Parole Boards cannot predict. I might add that a person's conduct in an institution is not an indication of what he will do after release. We have people who violate the rules and lose their good time, but that is not an indication they are bad risks afterwards. Conditions inside a prison and outside are very different. We set up the system using criteria from inside a prison to prevent people who are not necessarily the worst risks at all from getting out. We do not know who the worst risks are. I think it is fraudulent for Parliament to pass a Bill purporting to say that we will keep the high risk persons in prison, have experts decide whether or not they should be released, and as a result provide security. Experts cannot make those predictions. Psychologists have been trying for more than 100 years to make these kind of predictions and have not been able to do it successfully.
It is also important to ask ourselves whether keeping a "dangerous person" in prison until his warrant expiry date will even begin to deal with the problem of crime and violence. In the time between mandatory supervision and the warrant expiry date will that person become any less dangerous, whatever that means? What we can say for certain is that we will keep people in jail for longer periods of time, and that will contribute to the overcrowding problem and create further hostile feelings among the prisoners about the system. Clearly that is not what we want. We have overcrowded prisons already. The staff who have to deal with them already have enough problems on their hands. This is just another problem because it removes one of the incentives to good behaviour.
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
Neither will it provide us with any security afterwards. The John Howard Society suggests it will likely increase violence in prisons. It suggests that we look at the history of mandatory supervision and remission. Prior to 1971 there was no mandatory supervision. Prisoners were released as a result of remission with no form of supervision. Remission has been a part of the system for nearly 100 years. It has been a method of giving an incentive to people to behave in prison. It has served that function. Here we risk losing that.
The Canadian Council on Social Development has made interventions. Its proposals are constructive. It cares about the security of Canadians. It comes up with a list of recommendations for action, projects in the family, the community and the school. It wants to see implementation of family violence intervention programs, improved child care services, respitory care programs for single parents when they are not available, special programs to counteract the negative effects of family violence, positive parenting programs, community programs. All kinds of methods are at our disposal which will reduce the root causes of violence. They will work positively towards creating a more secure society.
In conclusion I simply want to say that this legislation is a fraud. It cannot do what it purports to do. It is falsely based and we have to go back to square one. We have to go back to positive measures to deal with violence and we should not be offering this illusion that more prisons and keeping people in them longer will provide anyone with any greater measure of security.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to continue my submissions on Bill C-67. I would first like to thank the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for her submissions. I listened very carefully to what she had to say and I must admit that I concur almost completely.
I would like to comment briefly on the history of this Bill and how the Government is dealing with it. Here we are at 7.25 p.m. on the day before the House adjourns for the summer. We have been sitting around on this legislation for over a year. I spoke on it last Wednesday evening. One would have thought, given the pronouncements of the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) over the last year, that he would bring this Bill back for debate the following day. When he spoke on Wednesday evening he indicated it was an important piece of legislation and that it was absolutely essential that it be passed as quickly as possible. Why then did he not bring it back on Thursday morning? The Government decided instead to go to other legislation, notwithstanding the pronouncements regarding the importance of this legislation.
The Bill deals with the concept of mandatory supervision. The guts of the Bill concern giving authority to the National Parole Board to decide whether or not an inmate should remain incarcerated until his or her warrant expiry. I indicated last Wednesday that the Official Opposition is generally supportive of the thrust of the legislation. In fact, the previous

June 26, 1986

Parole and Penitentiary Acts
Liberal Government introduced a Bill similar in nature. However, we do have a number of concerns, the major one being who should have the discretion to decide whether or not a detention order should be issued concerning a particular inmate. Under the present legislation, an inmate, after serving two-thirds of his or her sentence, is entitled to be released if he or she has been of good behaviour. Inmates can also be released on day parole after serving one-sixth of their sentence. The inmate would be released in the morning and return to the institution at night. The National Parole Board must conclude that the inmate is not a threat to society and that he or she is deserving of release on a daily basis.
An inmate is also entitled to apply for full parole after serving one-third of his or her sentence, and the same considerations apply when the National Parole Board is deciding whether or not to release an inmate after he has served one-third of his or her sentence.
There are those who are incarcerated in penitentiaries who are not released on day parole and who are not released on full parole, at least at the earliest eligibility date. There are those who are refused parole at first instance, but at some subsequent time re-apply for parole and are granted parole. There are those, however, who are not granted parole at all. These are inmates who, the National Parole Board decides, are a threat to society, or who have not conducted themselves in an appropriate fashion while incarcerated. They are forced, under the present legislation, to serve two-thirds of their sentence. After serving two-thirds of their sentence the inmate is released on condition. There are conditions attached to mandatory supervision, such as that the inmate might be required to remain in a particular community, or might not be permitted to associate with certain individuals or groups of individuals. The inmate might be required to report to the police or some other correctional authority on a weekly or daily basis.
It is important to note that under mandatory supervision once an inmate is released after serving two-thirds of the sentence there is a period of supervision. There is a period within which the authorities can exercise some form of control over the inmate. It is important that there be a period of time within which the necessary authorities can try to assist the inmate in rehabilitating himself or herself to assist the inmate in trying, once again, to lead a law-abiding life.
You can understand how important it is that there be a period of supervision, especially when an inmate has served a lengthy period of time. Let us take for example an inmate who has served 12 years in a penitentiary, who has been refused day parole, who has been refused full parole, and who is released on mandatory supervision. For 12 years this particular individual has been behind bars, has not had the opportunity to carry on a life that is law abiding, does not have the opportunity to do day-to-day things that we often take for granted. These might include such things as going to the corner grocery
store and purchasing some goods or groceries and making change, for example. If you serve 12 years in a federal penitentiary, it is a different world out there when you go out and try to assimilate back into society.
Mandatory supervision is a way of trying to assist individuals, of keeping an eye on inmates who are released by way of conditions. This particular concept of mandatory supervision was introduced in 1970. Now we have had 16 years of experience with regard to mandatory supervision, and while the whole concept is well intentioned and was considered to be a tremendous step in the right direction in terms of correctional philosophy and practices, we have found over the last 16 years that there are, indeed, problems associated with regard to mandatory supervision.
Many of the problems are perceived. Society generally is concerned about the release of inmates, and there have been a number of celebrated cases which have received considerable publicity, causing the public to call into question the area of mandatory supervision. Not only did the public question mandatory supervision, but they also started to question parole, not necessarily understanding the distinction between the release of inmates on mandatory supervision and the release of inmates on parole.
So, in effect, any of the shortcomings associated with mandatory supervision in a certain respect tainted the otherwise more successful parole system that exists in Canada.
We have had a number of cases over the last number of years that have caused considerable concern in the community. The Clifford Olson case, if I am correct, was one such case where the individual was released on mandatory supervision. There was a case about a year and a half ago where an individual, after serving a lengthy period of time in a federal penitentiary, was released on mandatory supervision and while out in society on mandatory supervision that particular individual committed a number of other murders. There was a great deal of concern in the community, so it was felt that the concept of mandatory supervision, as we know it, had to be amended in order to give the authorities-and I use that term loosely-more discretion to decide whether or not an inmate should be released.
Last Wednesday I referred to a discussion paper entitled "Mandatory Supervision", which was a report of the committee on mandatory supervision dated March 9, 1981. The Solicitor General of the time decided that it was important for his Department to study the whole concept of mandatory supervision.
It is a rather extensive report, and I commend it to Hon. Members opposite who have an interest in this whole area. I notice there are a number of Members opposite who are keenly interested in this particular debate. I know that at committee a great number of Members expressed an interest in this particular area. It begins with an introduction and a summary of mandatory supervision. It goes into the terms of reference which initiated this particular study. It speaks generally of the

study itself. It reaches certain conclusions to which I would like to refer a little later on. The report was published under the authority of the Hon. Bob Kaplan, former Solicitor General of Canada. The authors also looked into the history and objectives of mandatory supervision. They looked at the origins of mandatory supervision, the implementation of mandatory supervision, and the history of the legislative changes over the last 30 or 40 years or so. They made an in depth examination of the objectives of the MS program. They also compiled a number of statistics, which are very essential in considering this whole area. I would like to refer to those statistics, if I might, at this point in time.
They compared the difference between mandatory supervision and parole over a five-year period, in January of 1975 to December, 1979. At page 18 of this particular report they indicate the number of parole and mandatory supervision releases in 1973, 1974 and 1975.
The House will recall that last Wednesday the Solicitor General introduced third reading of Bill C-67. He indicated at the time that this particular legislation with regard to detention orders would only apply to a handful of inmates in federal penitentiaries. I believe the figure he used was approximately 100.
In order to keep the discussion in context, I think it is important to understand that we are only dealing here with approximately 100 individuals on an annual basis.
In 1973, there were 1,780 inmates who were released on mandatory supervision. In 1974, that number went up to 2,382, and in 1975, to 2,431. It is important to compare the number of releases on mandatory supervision with the number of releases on parole, and we are speaking of full parole. As I indicated, in 1973, there were 1,780 inmates released on mandatory supervision, compared with 1,191 who were released on parole. The comparative figures for 1974 are 2,382 released on mandatory supervision, and 1,359 released on parole. In 1975, 2,431 inmates were released on mandatory supervision, compared with 1,264 who were released on parole.
This tells us a number of things but, unfortunately, we do not have up to date statistics with regard to this particular matter. First, in that three year period, the number of inmates released on mandatory supervision increased on an annual basis from 1,780 to 2,382 to 2,431. On the other hand, the number of those released on full parole went up from 1,191 to 1,359, and back down to 1,264. Obviously, fewer inmates are released on full parole than are released on mandatory supervision.
Let us return to the figures for 1973. There were 1,780 released, of when 234 inmates had their mandatory supervision revoked without committing a new offence. In other words, they somehow breached a condition of mandatory supervision and for that reason 234 of the 1,780 were brought back into penitentiary because of a revocation without committing a new
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
offence. That amounts to 13.1 per cent who were brought back.
Of the 1,780 inmates released, 445 of those inmates, or 25 per cent, had their mandatory supervision revoked with a new offence. This means that while free on mandatory supervision, they committed a new offence contrary to the Criminal Code of Canada and were reincarcerated.
Of the 1,780 who were released in 1973, exactly 1,100 inmates, or 61.8 per cent, completed their mandatory supervision successfully. In 1973, a full 61.8 per cent completed the supervision period successfully and up until the time of the warrant expiry.
Let us examine the figures for 1974. There were 251 inmates who had their mandatory supervision revoked for breaching conditions that were attached to mandatory supervision. That represents 10.5 per cent. Six hundred and sixteen, or 25.9 per cent had their mandatory supervision revoked because of the commission of a new offence. There were 1,506 of the 2,382 who successfully completed their supervision.
In 1975, of the 2,431 inmates who were released on mandatory supervision, 329, or 13.5 per cent, had their mandatory supervision revoked without committing a new offence. Six hundred and twenty-three, or 25.6 per cent, had their mandatory supervision revoked for committing a new offence. One thousand four hundred and seventy-seven inmates, or 60.8 per cent, successfully completed their period of supervision.
It is interesting to note from these very limited statistics that over the course of this three year period, the figure with respect to those who successfully completed their period of mandatory supervision remained somewhat constant-from 61.8 per cent, to 63.2 per cent, to 60.8 per cent. I suggest that if we had more complete statistics, that particular experience would have continued since 1975, over the course of the last 11 years. There will always be about 60 per cent to 65 per cent of inmates who are released on mandatory supervision who successfully complete their period of supervision.

My colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), points out that that must save a lot of money. He is quite correct and perhaps I can divert from this subject for a moment to speak about the costs involved in incarcerating individuals in federal penitentiaries.
As all Hon. Members are aware, it costs in excess of $40,000 to incarcerate a federal inmate on an annual basis. That figure is increasing every year for each individual who is in a federal penitentiary.
The House will know that there are approximately 11,000 inmates in federal penitentiaries across Canada. That does not include those individuals who are incarcerated in provincial institutions for which, of course, the costs for incarceration are similar.

As I pointed out the other day, those individuals who commit criminal offences and are sentenced to a period of incarceration in excess of two years are sentenced to serve their time in federal penitentiaries, while those individuals who are given a sentence of less than two years serve their time in provincial institutions. Regardless of where an inmate serves his or her period of incarceration, there is a tremendous cost to society. Not only does it cost $40,000 to incarcerate an individual in a federal penitentiary, I am advised that it also costs in excess of $100,000 to build one new prison cell. Furthermore, that does not include costs of support services associated with running federal penitentiaries.
As Your Honour knows, a number of months ago the Nielsen task force made a number of recommendations regarding various federal Government programs. The task force examined close to 1,000 different federal programs. One area studied in particular was that of prisons and reformatories. The task force recommended and concluded that there should be a moratorium on all future construction of prisons in Canada and that there should in fact be a concerted effort on behalf of the federal Government to try to reduce the prison population. I would like to make some further submissions on that matter later.
The bottom line, to answer my friend, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis, is that it is extremely costly to keep inmates incarcerated and to run federal and provincial institutions in Canada so, where possible, it is important to try to reduce the prison population, not only to reduce costs to the taxpayers of Canada, but to assist in trying to rehabilitate certain people who are sentenced to federal prisons.
It is quite clear, given the over-abundance of evidence, that Canada has a higher rate of incarceration than most western democracies; but, as I pointed out when I was last speaking to this legislation, Canada also has one of the safest societies anywhere in the world. I suppose there will be those who argue that if the cost of a safe society is a higher rate of incarceration, then it is a cost that we should bear as taxpayers and as a society. However, I would submit that just because we incarcerate more individuals in Canada does not necessarily mean that the crime rate will drop.
I would like to return for a moment to the discussion paper and the statistics with regard to the release of individuals on mandatory supervision. It is important to compare the statistics of those released on mandatory supervision and those released on full parole. I was indicating that while approximately 60 per cent to 65 per cent of inmates released on mandatory supervision successfully complete their periods of supervision, we should compare that percentage with those on parole. You might ask, Mr. Speaker, and it would be a good question, "What is the percentage of individuals who are released on full parole who successfully complete their period of parole?"
I notice that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has been listening very attentively to my submissions. I believe he was also here the other night to listen to my submissions. I am sure he would be interested to know that in 1973, 68.5 per cent of those inmates released on full parole successfully completed their period of parole. In other words, while out on parole, their parole was not revoked, either for committing a new offence or for breaching a condition of release. In the same period, 61.8 per cent or 62 per cent of those on mandatory supervision successfully completed their period of supervision. So, the difference is not that great, mandatory supervision versus parole.
Let me make my case a little stronger and let me delve a little deeper into these statistics which are extremely enlightening, I found. Once again, I commend them to Hon. Members opposite. In 1974, of the 1,359 inmates released on full parole, the parole of 9.2 per cent was revoked for a breach of condition. The parole of 16.5 per cent was revoked after committing a new offence, and 69.6 per cent successfully completed their period of parole.
For 1975, the statistics are similar in nature. The parole of
11.1	per cent was revoked without a new offence having been committed. The parole of 14.3 per cent was revoked after a new offence having been committed, and 65.6 per cent successfully completed their period of parole.
What do these statistics tell? They tell a number of things. First, with respect to the number of people who successfully complete mandatory supervision, the figure is constant. With regard to those who successfully complete parole, once again, the figures are somewhat constant. However, what is important is that the figures for full parole are not that different from the figures for mandatory supervision. So, then, why do people argue, for example, that parole is far more successful than mandatory supervision if there is a similar percentage of those who are released on parole or mandatory supervision and successfully complete their period?
Some astute Hon. Members opposite might point out, if they took the time to study these statistics, that those who are released on mandatory supervision, of course, are not under supervision for as long a period of time as those who are released on parole. It only makes sense that they are not, because those who are released on mandatory supervision serve, at the very most, one-third of their sentence in the community, because they have been refused parole up until the two-thirds mark of their sentence. As well, there are many who are released on parole who serve a full two-thirds out in the community, having served only one-third of their sentence in the institution. Therefore, it could be argued that it is more difficult to successfully complete parole than it is to successfully complete mandatory supervision. However, before so arguing, it would be important to study some other important statistics that I believe tell the tale. If Hon. There were 17 other forms of assault in the first category versus 153 in the other. There were six kidnappings versus 15. There were 127 robberies committed by those on parole and 394 committed by those on mandatory supervision.
With regard to convictions for robbery, of those released on parole that figure represents 18 per cent of the total whereas only 15 per cent of the total inmates released on mandatory supervision committed robbery. In fact, more individuals released on parole were convicted of robbery than individuals released on mandatory supervision.
The statistics are similar with regard to crimes against property. There were 192 convictions of break and enter of those out on parole versus 737 of those out on mandatory supervision. Even though the figure is higher, it only represents 28 per cent versus 27 per cent.
The bottom line of this particular chart is that there is not that much difference on a percentage basis between crimes committed by those released on mandatory supervision and crimes committed by those released on parole. However, the absolute numbers are important.
Among those released on mandatory supervision, there were 52 homicides. The question we must then ask is if Bill C-67 was in effect between 1975 and December 1979, could we have saved any of those 52 lives? I suspect that we could have. If the authorities had the discretion to keep incarcerated inmates that were believed to continue to pose a threat to society, those inmates who committed the 52 homicides might not have had the opportunity to do so. Perhaps they would have remained incarcerated. Sooner or later, however, those inmates who committed those crimes would have to be released even if this legislation were in effect. That particular fact seems to have escaped the Solicitor General.
When the Solicitor General made his submissions on this Bill, he seemed to suggest that the Bill would somehow ensure the protection of society from those inmates who would be released and would commit more crimes. At no point in time did the Solicitor General express a concern or opinion with respect to what would happen to those individuals after they were released. There was not even a recognition of the fact
that sooner or later, these inmates would have to be released into society.
If we are to keep inmates incarcerated to warrant expiry, until they have served their complete sentences, do we not think that these particular inmates will be that much angrier with society and that much more vindictive? What guarantees do we have that society will be safer just because these inmates were kept incarcerated for a longer period of time? The unfortunate reality is that we cannot provide that guarantee. However, I suppose the guarantee we as parliamentarians can provide is that at least for a further period of time, be it two years, five years or six years, a particular inmate will be kept incarcerated and will not have the opportunity to commit a new crime.
It seems to me that in many respects, we are simply prolonging the inevitable. Sooner or later, these inmates will be released into society. It seems to me that we as a society should concentrate our collective efforts on trying to rehabilitate those incarcerated in institutions to try to ensure that they do not become recidivists, commit another crime and be readmitted to institutions.
How do we rehabilitate these people? I feel that more effort could be spent on that. For hundreds of years, penologists have studied the treatment of offenders and the prevention of crime but they have not been able to eradicate crime from society. I would submit, though, that tremendous steps have been taken in the correctional area over the last 25 or 50 years and indeed, because of the efforts of society, the rate of recidivism has in fact been reduced.
As I indicated at second reading stage, in committee and on a number of occasions already, this legislation is a step in the right direction as far as the Opposition is concerned. I know that the New Democratic Party as represented by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) opposes this legislation in a very definite way. In fact, I believe members of the New Democratic Party intend to vote against this legislation.
I would like to indicate why we believe this legislation is a step in the right direction. We recognize that there is a problem. We have seen the statistics and we have seen what happens when inmates are released on mandatory supervision. Our inevitable conclusion is that there is a problem and that problem must be addressed. The former Solicitor General, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), recognized the problem a number of years ago and introduced legislation designed to deal with it.
It is clear that we simply cannot release into society inmates who pose a clear threat to society. We as Parliamentarians have an obligation to ensure that legislation is in place to somehow keep incarcerated those who pose a clear threat to society. I would submit, though, that those individuals are few in number and represent a small percentage of the total number of inmates in federal institutions.
June 26, 1986

The legislation gives the National Parole Board the power to order detention until warrant expiry of any inmate who meets the criteria set out in the legislation itself. As I indicated at some length on June 18, we in the Liberal Party believe very strongly that that power or discretion ought to be properly exercised by a court of law. We do not believe that the National Parole Board, given its collective wisdom, experience, and expertise in this particular area, should be in a position to deprive an individual of his or her liberty. We do not believe that the National Parole Board should do it because it is not a court of law. Only a court should deprive an individual of his or her liberty. We also believe that procedural safeguards exist when a court of law is making that determination. We can be assured that the process will in fact be followed if a court of law makes the decision.
We all know that the National Parole Board, during the course of the Conservative mandate, seems to have been rendered the happy hunting ground for Tory hacks, flacks, and Party supporters. The sister-in-law of the Secretary of State for Exernal Affairs (Mr. Clark) was appointed to the National Parole Board. Other prominent Conservatives have also been appointed to that board. I am not calling into question, at least not at this point in time, the abilities of the individuals who have been appointed to the National Parole Board. However, the fact remains that as far as the public is concerned, there might be a perception that it is pure and blatant patronage when individuals are appointed to the board.
Bill C-67 increases the number of people who can sit on the board. The point I am making is that although these people gain a considerable amount of expertise while sitting on the board, they should not be put in a position where they have to decide whether or not an inmate should be kept incarcerated.
As I indicated a few moments ago, the Bill will allow the National Parole Board to issue detention orders. It is true that the legislation provides that that particular order is reviewable after a year's time. Once again, an inmate can apply to be released after a year. Notwithstanding that the inmate is allowed a review after a year, we still firmly believe that it is a decision which ought to be made by the courts.
We have another concern with regard to the nature of the discretion. Criteria are established by the legislation and indeed are set out in it. The National Parole Board does not have a blanket, carte blanche discretion to decide which inmates should not be released on mandatory supervision. Certain criteria are enunciated in the legislation, and the National Parole Board, the deciding body, must refer to those criteria.
An inmate could be identified as posing a high risk to public safety if he or she meets the criteria set out in the Parole Act. The first criterion in the legislation refers to whether the current offence for which the offender was convicted resulted in serious personal harm such as loss of life or major physical or psychological damage. At first instance the National Parole
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
Board must look at those inmates who are presently incarcerated and are about to be released on mandatory supervision. It will be specifically looking at those who were convicted of offences which resulted in serious personal harm such as loss of life or major physical or psychological damage. There is a Schedule attached to Bill C-67 which outlines the offences.
For example, if an inmate is serving time for committing manslaughter, the National Parole Board will decide whether or not a detention order should issue. Manslaughter is one of the offences listed in the Schedule attached to the Bill. I should like to point out very briefly the offences to which the National Parole Board must refer in order to determine which inmates should be kept incarcerated. It will look at all inmates convicted of causing injury with intent, a breach of Section 83 of the Criminal Code, the use of a firearm during the commission of an offence, pointing a firearm, a prison breach, manslaughter, attempted murder, assault causing bodily harm, overcoming resistence, assault, assault with a weapon, causing bodily harm, aggravated assault, unlawfully causing bodily harm, assaulting a police officer, sexual assault, sexual assault with a weapon, threats to a third party, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, robbery, arson-setting fire to another substance-setting fire by negligence, and conspiracy to commit murder.
If an inmate is serving a period of incarceration for having committed one of these crimes, then he or she satisfies the first criterion laid out in the legislation. Once those particular inmates are identified, the National Parole Board must decide whether reasonable grounds exist to conclude that the person is likely to commit, prior to the expiry of his or her sentence, a violent crime which will result in harm.
As I pointed out the last time we discussed this Bill, one cannot predict with any degree of certainty whether an individual is likely to commit a violent crime which will result in harm. That simply cannot be done. At committee the experts told us that it was near impossible to predict violent behaviour with any degree of certainty. That is not to suggest that we should not at least try. In order to ensure that society is protected, it is important for authorities, to the best of their ability, to predict or decide whether a person is likely to commit a violent crime that will result in harm. If an inmate is serving a person of incarceration for having committed a crime enumerated in the Schedule, and the National Parole Board decides that reasonable grounds exist to conclude that the person is likely to commit a crime, then a detention order will issue. This means that the inmate will not automatically be released on mandatory supervision.
There is a further provision in the Bill which caused us some concern. Of course we indicated our concerns at committee. With regard to the discretion given to the Commissioner of Corrections in the sense that even if an inmate does not meet the first criteria, that is the inmate has not been incarcerated for a crime that is enumerated in the Schedule, the Commissioner of Corrections, as long as he has reasonable grounds to believe an inmate is likely to commit, prior to the expirty of

June 26, 1986
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
sentence, a violent crime that will result in violent harm, he may refer the case to the Chairman of the National Parole Board for a detention hearing. This legislation is giving a lot of power to the Commissioner of Corrections. If someone is serving a period of incarceration for, let us say, a crime against property, break and enter, and there are reasonable grounds to believe-whatever that means, that is a pretty loose standard-as long as the Commissioner believes or has reasonable grounds to believe that an inmate might be violent if released, he may refer the case to the Chairman of the National Parole Board for a detention hearing.
We do not believe that the Commissioner of Corrections should have that discretion. We believe the criteria with regard to the type of crime an inmate has committed should be restricted to those inmates who are serving time for having committed crimes against the person. As you know, inmates who do not meet the criteria as I have indicated that are outlined in Clause 2 of the Bill, but are not judged to pose a high risk and are released on mandatory supervision, will not be entitled to a remission again if that first release is revoked by the Parole Board.
I spoke at some length on this issue last day. It is referred to as "one shot mandatory supervision". This provision in the Bill will effectively allow inmates only one chance for release. In other words, if the inmate is released and breaches a condition of mandatory supervision, then that inmate will not be able to earn remission after the inmate is reincarcerated.
I know the hour is late and Hon. Members are anxious to do whatever they plan to do after they leave the hallowed halls of Parliament. I have spoken at some length on Bill C-67, and so I now intend to conclude my remarks.

One of my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) said that Members opposite are truly appreciative of my submissions. I would like to thank him.
Seriously speaking, Mr. Speaker, we do not intend to obstruct this legislation. We have not in any way obstructed
the passage of it. We were anxious when this Bill was introduced in June, 1985 to deal with it. We expedited second reading debate. The legislation was referred to committee. The Official Opposition was very responsible and constructive at committee, suggesting some very worth-while points. We listened attentively to all the individuals and groups who appeared before the committee and we expedited passage through committee.
This Bill was reported out of committee over five months ago. The Government and the Solicitor General have sat on this legislation since that time. Then they have unmitigated audacity to tell the House of Commons, with a few precious hours remaining in this session of Parliament before the summer break that the legislation is important, urgent and ought to be passed immediately.
I would like to say through you to the Solicitor General and the Government opposite, Mr. Speaker, that the Official Opposition resents very much the way the Government is operating. The Government has had ample opportunity to bring this Bill forward over the last five months but has refused to do so. Be that as it may, the legislation is a step in the right direction. We intend to support it. Of course, we cannot give any guarantees as to what the Senate might do with this Bill. The Senate has expressed its opinion on a number of occasions by way of several reports that have been passed on to the House. The Senate will deal with the Bill when it is referred there.
I would like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to speak to this Bill. I know you have given me ample opportunity to speak to the very serious concerns of Bill C-67. Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the passage of this Bill. In fact, we want to pass it very quickly this evening. I would, however, like to give this explanation.
Bill C-68 addresses concerns of a more technical nature than Bill C-67. It, nonetheless, contains important changes to the conditional release statutes which are long overdue.
