Mr. Speaker, during Question Period on May 27 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) if he would consider amending the provisions of the Income Tax Act to make available the tax free intergenerational roll-over of farm land to those Canadians who have farmed almost all their lives but who, through illness or advancing age, are not now actively farming. I wish to utilize this opportunity to expand on the question because the legislation is complex and because there appears to be confusion between the definition of land qualifying for the lifetime $500,000 capital gains exemption and the definition of lands qualifying for the intergenerational roll-over.
The problem in each instance relates to the capital gains tax which was instituted in 1972 and has since been viewed with less than enthusiasm by the farm community. Farm land was valued as at valuation day, December 31, 1971, and carried this value as an adjusted cost base for calculation of future gains. It also happened that farm land values escalated very rapidly through the 1970s and, although values are now dropping owing to discouraging world commodity prices, there remains today the potential for considerable capital gain to arise in the event of some dispositions.

June 26, 1986
Adjournment Debate
The outrage of the farm community to capital gain was sufficiently strong that modifications were made to the Act on several occasions. In 1973 provision was made for a tax free roll-over between parent and child so that in the traditional family farm situation the parent could elect to transfer title to his land to a child at the parents adjusted cost base without tax provided the land was, at the time of the transaction, being used by either parent or any child in the business of farming.
The requirement that the particular land be used in the business of farming at the time of the transaction has caused considerable problems. This requirement led to the widespread usage of custom work contracts. Through the custom work contracts the traditional lease situation was converted into a contractual arrangement on paper so that the elderly or retired owner of land was still able to satisfy Revenue Canada that he or she was using the land in the business of farming. This was done by demonstrating through the custom work contract that the owner still made certain management decisions relating to the land, held a current delivery permit book, received the proceeds of the crop, wrote cheques for various custom work operations and generally assumed some degree of risk.
Meanwhile, however, those unfortunate people who were unaware of the subtleties of the law and simply leased their land to neighbours, either for crop share or cash, and then in good faith proceeded to transfer their titles to their children, found themselves subject to capital gains tax. Land owners in similar circumstances who died were deemed to have disposed of their land at fair market value at the date of death and their estates were, in turn, subject to capital gains.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, the enactment of the immediate $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption for farmers was welcomed by all concerned with agriculture. The capital gains exemption is available to those who are either actively farming the particular land at the date of the deal or who have farmed that land for any five years. This is obviously quite a wide definition which accommodates those Canadians who may have farmed most of their lives but who are retired or inactive at the time of the disposition or who, on death, became subject to the deemed disposition provisions.
The problem today is that so much publicity and attention has been given to the lifetime capital gains exemption that many Canadians believe the intergenerational roll-over between parent and child is likewise to be available on the same conditions. That is, where land is being farmed by transferor at the date of the deal or for any five years during which the land was owned by him. In fact that is not so. The tax free roll-over is available only where either parent or a child is actively farming the land. If neither is involved, the roll-over does not apply even though the transferor may have farmed the particular land most or all of his life.
With respect, I believe the definition of land eligible for the intergenerational roll-over should be expanded so as to be the same as the definition of land qualifying for the lifetime
capital gains exemption. This could be done by applying the definition of "qualifying farm property" prescribed under Section 110.6(1) of the Income Tax Act to Section 70 and Section 73 which govern the transfer of farm property by parent to child either inter vivos or on death. In other words, add the five-year usage clause to the roll-over criteria.
Some say this is not an important or pressing matter because the lifetime capital gains exemption is still available to those who might unwittingly find themselves ineligible for the intergenerational roll-over. Therefore, it is only those Canadians with in excess of $500,000 capital gains who would be affected. Unfortunately, the tentacles of the alternative minimum tax enter into the picture. While it is true that in almost all situations any tax paid under those provisions would be recovered as a credit against future tax payable, nonetheless there has to be payment up front and future recovery over a period of years. Furthermore, I am advised that the AMT payable by a deceased's estate on a deemed disposition can only offset tax paid during the previous three years.
Clearly there are some additional complications for those who have not had proper advice. However, the fact remains that there is no logical reason for the distinction, and the difference in the definitions of land qualifying. Those in the know can still structure their affairs through phoney custom work contracts and artificial contrivances. Why put them to the trouble? Why not put all farmers on the same footing? Why should it matter one iota whether the land is custom farmed or rented for crop sharing or cash? Why not simplify the Act by standardizing the definition, thereby removing an irritating impediment to effective farm state planning and management?
I see my time is almost up. I thank you for this opportunity to elaborate on this problem. I again urge the Minister to consider amending the provisions of the Income Tax Act to make available the tax free roll-over to those Canadians who have farmed for a considerable part of their lives, but who, through illness or advancing age, find that they are not now actively farming and therefore not eligible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson) who asked whether the rules concerning the intergenerational roll-over of farm land could be applied to something which has already been used by the taxpayer in the operation of the farm but which, for one reason or another, was not used immediately before the roll-over.
As the Hon. Member pointed out, Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced that the lifetime $500,000 capital gains tax exemption would be immediately available to farmers, a special provision was made concerning farm lands which were not in use at that time, provided they had been used during at least five years in the past.
June 26, 1986

However the inter-generational roll-over of farm land differs from the capital gains tax exemption in several respects. First, as you know, Mr. Speaker, the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption is available to all Canadians, whereas the special provision for farmers does nothing more than speed up the process.
Therefore the distinction between active and inactive farm land does not matter much because the roll-over is restricted to two successive generations and applies only to farmers.
The purposes of these two measures are also quite different. The capital gains tax exemption is meant as a reward for individuals who have made successful investments and an incentive to make more investments.
On the other hand, the roll-over provisions apply not only to capital gains but also to depreciation and gains from eligible real estate, the idea being to encourage active farm land rollover from one generation to the next. This objective is achieved by deferring taxes which would otherwise be payable with respect to the roll-over and which might reduce the assets and compromise the profitability of the operation. In this way, cashflow problems in connection with tax payable on intergenerational roll-over of farmland are avoided.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) agrees to a certain extent with the specific example given by the Hon. Member, referring to taxpayers who have stopped operating their farm due to illness or advancing age. It is difficult to make a distinction between these and other cases where the owner of the land was not farming.
In view of these considerations and especially the fact that up to one-half million dollars in capital gain per person would be tax-extempt in any case, I don't think it would be desirable, for the time being, to broaden the application of provisions governing the inter-generational roll-over of eligible farm property.
Nervertheless, as the Hon. Member is well aware, this Government is very much interested in ensuring that the Canadian family farm remains viable, as demonstrated by the many measures we took previously in this area.
Mr. Speaker, it was with this principle in mind that the Minister of Finance said on May 27 of this year that he would take another look at the proposal. I would therefore urge the Hon. Member to continue his positive contribution towards the development of a satisfactory system for the inter-generational roll-over of farm property.

Mr. Speaker, on June 17 I put a question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Valcourt). I asked what Revenue Canada is doing to ensure that public confidence is maintained in the charity sector in view of the creation by the Canadian Council of Better Business Bureaus
Adjournment Debate
of philanthropic advisory services. The BBB apparently saw the need for such a watch-dog service to protect consumers by providing information on which charities meet their standards. The Bureau commented that Revenue Canada does an inadequate job of policing Canada's 50,000 plus registered charities. Both the Consumers' Association of Canada and the umbrella National Voluntary Organization, on the other hand, are aware of the role played by Revenue Canada, and that public awareness of this audit and monitoring role may be misunderstood as Revenue Canada can only advise that audits are carried out and all complaints are treated seriously and followed up. Confidentiality provisions preclude dissemination of information concerning an audit action on a particular charity.
The charities are critical of the means by which the BBB plans to attack perceived abuse by a very small number of registered charities and those entities that hold themselves out as registered. It is evident that the public should be fully informed of the extent of the audit and monitoring role played by Revenue Canada in this area. I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to discuss this with the Minister to ensure that Revenue Canada not only perform this vital function, but also that the public is informed as to the nature and extent of this function.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to mention that volunteer organizations would like to receive more tangible recognition that would act as an incentive to further develop and renew their work in the community. In fact, the organizations are complaining today about "burn-out" among their members.
Mr. Speaker, I have asked for a special committee to be set up to make an in-depth study of the role of volunteers in Canada and to report to the Minister of Finance and the Department of the Secretary of State with recommendations on the best way for this Government to encourage more Canadian men and women to get more involved.
Mr. Speaker, our population is aging, and it will not be long before we need more room to house the elderly. The State will no longer be able to provide. We will need, as a society, the involvement of volunteers in our communities. Mr. Speaker, I think we should look at what other countries do for their volunteers.
In the United States, for instance, since we are in the middle of free trade talks, Mr. Bruce Davies, a tax adviser for the U. S. Congress Ways and Means Committee, told me that the United States now has a tax incentive for volunteer work, which means that all personal expenses in connection with a volunteer program or job may be deducted as a direct contribution from one's income tax. For instance, they can deduct 12 cents a mile for trips made to provide volunteer services and they can also deduct the cost of uniforms purchased by a service organization. Just think, Mr. Speaker, how little things like that could help out Canadian voluteers continue their work in their community.

June 26, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, there is also an organization in the United States that is called Action, and President Reagan hopes that it will be an incentive to companies and individuals to provide a public service on a volunteer basis instead of letting the Government do it.
Before I finish, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I was just at a meeting with some women who told us about their problems in connection with the financing of women's groups. These are all volunteers who every day try to help women that are less fortunate that they are. Mr. Speaker, in my riding a centre for women in need was recently set up, and I must say that without volunteer help, these women would never be able to receive a service that is extremely important, especially in remote areas like mine. I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, that this Government will find a way to encourage more volunteeers to get involved and help their less-fortunate fellow citizens. I hope that the concerns raised by the Quebec Trade Practices Commission will receive a logical response, and I am very happy to have been able to take part in the adjournment debate this evening. Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may take this opportunity to urge you to look around this summer in your riding at what is happening to volunteer work and when you come back in September perhaps you and I could support a request to the Minister for tax incentives for our organizations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to explain the role of Revenue Canada Taxation concerning the registration and control of charitable organizations.
In applying for registration, an applicant has to provide information that is sufficiently clear and detailed for departmental officials to determine whether the organization is, in fact, charitable at law, and whether the Income Tax Act's operational requirements for registered charities will be satisfied.
Great care is taken in reviewing applications. Where they feel it is necessary, officials of the Department will request further information and, where appropriate, encourage representatives of the applicant organization to meet with them.

Registration acceptance or refusal must not be considered as a judgment on the value of the activities and goals of the organization or of the motives of the individuals involved. The legislation only allows the department to make sure that the benefits offered to charitable organizations registered under the Income Tax Act are available only to those organizations which intend to operate in accordance with the rules established under tax legislation and common law.

After an organization has registered, it is required by law to file each year an information return containing a confidential accounting of its entire operations during the last year. A percentage of these information returns are reviewed and, where appropriate, further inquiries are made. This is the same as the review process that applies to regular tax returns.
Every charitable organization must provide annually a public information return containing financial information. Copies of these returns are made available to the public on request. This procedure does not preclude interested parties from also obtaining information directly from the charity itself or from provincial regulatory bodies.
Every year the Department carries out a number of audits and investigations on the basis of information on its files or supplied by the public. The departmental reviews that are made of certain charities include examination of some of the following matters; amount of receipted donations spent on charitable activities to ensure that the dispersement quota as required by income tax legislation is being met; adherence to filing and public disclosure requirements; a review of charitable activities to ensure that the legal definition of charity is still being met; a review of political activities to ensure that they are incidental and ancillary to the organization's charitable activities, and a review of receipting policies and procedures.
A number of refinements in administration have been put in place in the last year, after consultation with the voluntary sector. These include new and clearer explanations of how to register a charity, as well as new and simpler annual reporting requirements.
The Department is satisfied that the overwhelming majority of charitable organizations carry out their admirable work fully within the law. However, all complaints are treated seriously and, if warranted, are acted upon.
If a charitable organization is found to be overstepping the boundaries of charities, or is in breach of the technical rules contained in the Income Tax Act, the Department makes every effort to encourage it to correct the situation.
The ultimate step of revoking an organization's registration is, we have found, seldom necessary. In fact, only 18 charities have had their registered status revoked for cause in the past 12 years, whereas some 1,200 organizations are deregistered annually for administrative and other reasons.

subtopic: CHALLENGE '86-FUNDING OF SOCIAL SERVICE PROJECTS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIORITY BE GIVEN TO SOCIALLY USEFUL EMPLOYMENT

speechtext:
Hon. Warren AUmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on May 26 I put a question to the Minister for summer employment. While I believe her official title is Minister for Youth, since she has no other responsibility
June 26, 1986

but summer employment, I suggest it is more accurate to call her the Minister for summer employment.
In any event, on May 26 I put the question to her with respect to the funding of Challenge '86, the summer employment program of the Government. On that day, a coalition of community groups from across the country met with her and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), to protest the fact that funding for a large number of community groups in this country for summer employment projects had been cut or had been eliminated altogether.
For example, in Montreal, the Association for Retarded Children, which has been funded in past years for approximately 30 people to take care of retarded children at summer camp, had been cut back to five or six. As a result, a large number of retarded children will not be going to camp.
There were other community groups that had also been cut. These include groups helping senior citizens, community groups helping disadvantaged youth, as well as community groups working on environmental projects. An important project in my riding was one which helped young people with drug problems. That was cut back altogether, with no funding at all.
There are two reasons why so many of these groups were left without funding or were seriously cut back. One is the cut in total funding for the summer employment program by $19 million over last year. In 1985, Challenge 85 had a budget of $205 million. For 1986, the budget is $188 million.
If that is not bad enough, in addition to this cut in funds, the Government also introduced a quota system. I call it a quota system because that is what it really is. It is a quota system which allocated a greater percentage of that money to the private business sector. The Government used these public funds to assist private business with their summer employment programs. Of course, this left the community groups, who have no other source of funding except governments and charitable organizations, short of money.
I asked the Minister to reconsider these quotas and cuts and restore the program to the way it was so that these worth-while groups could get funding. She made no reply, except to suggest in her answer that I was totally opposed to students getting jobs in the summer. That is ridiculous. Of course, I am for students getting jobs. I want them to have meaningful employment and, at the same time, I want that employment to provide useful social work in the community.
Despite her suggestions to the contrary, I would admit that there are some good jobs being funded under the present program. Of course, when the Government spends $188 million some good jobs will obviously be funded. That is not the point of my criticism or the criticism of the groups which came to see the Minister that day. The point is that the Government cut back and put in place a priority which gave more money to the private sector which, I maintain, it did not need.
Adjournment Debate
In the past, the criteria for summer employment projects was to provide some socially useful services. That is no longer the criteria. Therefore, we now have summer employment projects where people are cutting grass on golf courses, piling boxes on shelves, serving ice cream and other such things. These are worth-while, but public funds should not be given in order that they be accomplished. People will sell ice-cream in the summertime, anyway; people will cut their grass in the summertime, anyway, and they will pay people to do it.
If we consider the pattern of funding of this program over the last few years, we will see that in 1984, under the Summer Employment Program, $126.4 million went to the community sector. In 1985, the amount to the community sector went down to $116.8 million. This year, under the SEED program, which is part of Challenge '86, it has gone down to $82.55 million. Furthermore, if we consider the pattern as to how the average grant works out, we will see that in 1985 the average grant for community organizations was $15,600 and in 1986 it is down to $8,800. The average number of work weeks funded under the Challenge 85 program for community groups was 66.5 weeks, and in 1986 it is down to 36.2 weeks.
These criticisms that I bring to the House, contrary to what the Minister says, are not my own criticisms. She tries to pretend that these are the criticisms of people in the Opposition and that we are criticizing simply to be negative. I have seen editorial after editorial and have received letters from group after group making these criticisms, and I make them on their behalf.
My allotted time has just about finished. I will sit down. I had expected that the Minister, who is only a junior Minister, would have been here to answer my criticism; but, no, we will probably receive an answer from some Parliamentary Secretary who is not even familiar with the dossier but who will read a set piece prepared by some bureaucrat in the Department of Employment and then sit down without even understanding what he is reading to me. Our only hope in these debates is that we can reach beyond this Parliament and touch the people outside, sensitizing them so they know what is really going on in this country with respect to summer employment and other job-creation programs.

subtopic: CHALLENGE '86-FUNDING OF SOCIAL SERVICE PROJECTS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIORITY BE GIVEN TO SOCIALLY USEFUL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of State (Youth) (Mrs. Champagne), I would like to give the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) a more specific answer to the question he raised last May 26. The quality of elements in the new job planning, Challenge '86, is designed to create jobs which will give students practical work experience and training which will ease their transition from school to the labour market. In that respect, the private sector plays a leading role since in any event it will hire graduating students seeking permanent jobs.

June 26, 1986
Adjournment Debate

Mr. Speaker, I am familiar with this dossier. I am aware of the good work that Challenge '86 has done in my own riding. It does not make sense to rely only upon the non-private sector to assist in providing the employment, training and experience young people need. The private sector is the engine of our impressive economic recovery, and the Government wants to encourage economic renewal by training our young people to enter this dynamic new labour market rather than allowing them to be left behind.
The summer programs of the previous Government relied upon the non-private sector to meet the employment needs of young people; but Challenge '86 puts the employment needs of young people first. However, the Government is not discriminating against the non-private sector through the Challenge '86 program. Under Challenge '86, students will work for organizations concerned with alcohol abuse, battered women and the mentally retarded, and will also support community recreational activities and child-care services. In fact, some 64.9 per cent of the funds are still being provided to the non-private sector, as compared with 35.1 per cent for the private sector. However, many of the jobs provided by the nonprivate sector not only promote community services but also
offer training and work experience that will benefit students when they eventually seek permanent employment. That fact is a key to the success of our summer programming. All applications are assessed equally, whether they are from the private or non-private sectors, and are judged on the basis of the quality of the training and work experience that they provide and how they enhance the career prospects of students.
Challenge '86 calls upon the private and non-private sectors to propose jobs which will help students make the school-to-work transition, jobs that will provide real employment experiences and training in areas that are related to what they are taking in school and therefore benefit their future entry into the exciting labour market of the 1980s.
